headline: ECB’s Schnabel Warns Germany’s Export-Driven Growth Model Is No Longer Viable
html_content:
ECB Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel warned that Germany’s traditional export-driven growth model is no longer viable in a fragmented global economy, arguing that persistent weakness in domestic demand, rather than simply deteriorating export competitiveness, is the fundamental problem behind the country’s prolonged stagnation. Speaking at the Bank of Lithuania’s Economics Conference in Vilnius on Friday, Schnabel noted that Germany’s real GDP per capita fell by 0.5% between 2019 and 2024. While protectionism, elevated energy costs and competition from China have created substantial challenges, she argued that Germany’s export performance has broadly followed global trends rather than suffering an exceptional collapse. “Especially in a more fragmented world, its export-driven business model is no longer viable,” she said.

Schnabel pointed to decades of subdued household spending and investment as the deeper structural weakness. Real private consumption has grown by less than 1% annually on average since 1999, partly reflecting reforms in the early 2000s that deliberately restrained real wage growth. These policies increased corporate profits and savings, contributing to persistent current account surpluses, while insufficient domestic investment meant much of the accumulated capital was deployed abroad. Despite substantial trade surpluses, Germany’s economy grew by only 1.4% annually on average between 1999 and 2019. “The key shortfall, therefore, is not a collapse in external demand or a unique deterioration in competitiveness,” Schnabel said. “Rather, it is a sustained weakness in domestic demand that makes Germany’s economy more prone than others to crises abroad.”

Looking ahead, Schnabel welcomed Germany’s major fiscal expansion, describing it as “the largest since the Second World War” and “a welcome step in the right direction.” She argued that well-targeted public investment in infrastructure, defence and digital transformation, accompanied by structural reforms, could strengthen domestic demand while raising the economy’s productive capacity. Such measures could also encourage German companies to invest more at home rather than expanding production abroad. The challenge is to shift Germany toward a more domestically supported growth model without sacrificing its industrial strengths, creating a more resilient economy in an environment of fragmented global trade.

Full speech of ECB’s Schnabel here.

headline: Eurozone Trade Swings to Deficit as Energy Costs Rise and EU Manufacturing Surplus Shrinks
html_content:
Eurozone goods trade recorded a €10.3B deficit in September 2026, reversing a €13.5B surplus a year earlier, according to Eurostat. Exports increased 6.0% yoy to €272.7B, but imports surged 16.1% to €283.0B, reflecting a substantial imbalance between the growth of external sales and purchases. The deterioration was driven primarily by a widening energy deficit, which increased from €20.7B to €33.0B, alongside a narrowing machinery and vehicles surplus from €10.0B to €3.0B. Although the unadjusted deficit improved from €16.6B in August, the seasonally adjusted balance deteriorated from a €7.8B deficit to €8.7B, suggesting that the underlying monthly trade position weakened slightly.

The broader European Union recorded a €16.8B trade deficit, compared with an €11.4B surplus in September 2025, as exports rose 4.7% yoy while imports jumped 17.9%. The €28.2B deterioration was not solely an energy story, as Europe’s traditional manufacturing trade surpluses also narrowed considerably. The EU energy deficit widened from €24.1B to €37.6B, accounting for almost half of the overall deterioration. Meanwhile, the machinery and vehicles surplus shrank from €13.1B to €3.3B, with imports rising 22.5% against export growth of 8.0%. The chemicals surplus also declined from €26.0B to €19.0B, as chemical exports contracted 13.5%. Together, these developments reduced the EU’s manufactured goods surplus from €32.4B to €15.8B.

Trade performance with major partners highlighted further pressures. The EU’s surplus with the US nearly halved from €21.3B to €10.9B, as exports to the US fell 10.6% yoy while imports increased 14.7%. Its deficit with China widened from €35.2B to €41.7B, reflecting a 12.2% increase in imports against a 1.4% decline in exports. The deficit with Norway also expanded from €2.1B to €6.3B amid a 60.1% surge in imports, consistent with the broader rise in energy import costs. In contrast, trade surpluses with the UK and Switzerland improved. The wider deterioration extended well beyond a single month: during January–September, the Eurozone shifted from a €102.2B surplus in 2025 to a €36.5B deficit in 2026, while the EU moved from an €85.5B surplus to an €83.2B deficit. The figures underscore the combined pressure of higher import costs and weakening manufacturing trade balances, although nominal trade values alone cannot distinguish price effects from changes in traded volumes.

  • Eurozone trade reversed from a €13.5B surplus to a €10.3B deficit, as import growth significantly outpaced exports.
  • The EU’s trade deterioration extended beyond energy, with machinery, vehicles and chemicals contributing to a substantial reduction in manufacturing surpluses.
  • EU trade balances weakened sharply with the US and China, while stronger surpluses with the UK and Switzerland provided some offset.

headline: US PPI Slows Sharply to 0.3%, but Underlying Price Pressures Stay Firm
html_content:
US producer prices rose 0.3% mom in October, slowing sharply from an upwardly revised 1.4% in September and coming in below market expectations of 0.4%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. September’s increase was revised up from 1.3%. Despite the monthly moderation, annual PPI inflation accelerated from 6.3% to 6.5%, slightly below expectations of 6.6% but marking its highest level since November 2022. More importantly, the index excluding food, energy and trade services increased 0.5% mom for the second consecutive month, with its annual rate reaching 4.9%. The contrasting readings suggest that the sharp slowdown in headline producer inflation has yet to translate into convincing relief in underlying price pressures.

The moderation was evident across both goods and services, although important pockets of inflation persisted. Final demand goods prices slowed from 2.5% to 0.5% mom, with energy prices edging down 0.1%. However, food prices rose 1.3%, while goods excluding food and energy increased 0.5%, accounting for more than 60% of the overall goods price advance. Basic organic chemicals prices jumped 3.9%, even as diesel fuel fell 7.9%. Meanwhile, final demand services inflation eased from 1.0% to 0.2%, its fifth consecutive monthly increase. Transportation and warehousing costs rose 2.0%, led by a 3.9% increase in truck freight prices, which accounted for more than 80% of the overall rise in final demand services. Declining trade services margins provided a partial offset.

Further along the production chain, price developments also showed an uneven picture. Processed goods for intermediate demand increased 0.4% mom, while intermediate services prices rose 0.6%. In contrast, unprocessed goods prices declined 3.1%, primarily reflecting lower energy costs, including a 10.3% fall in crude petroleum prices. Nevertheless, annual inflation in processed intermediate goods reached 14.6%, while intermediate services prices were up 6.8% yoy, highlighting persistent cost pressures beyond raw energy inputs. Overall, October’s PPI offers some relief from September’s exceptionally strong monthly increase, but not clear evidence of a broad-based easing in producer inflation. The combination of firm underlying prices, elevated intermediate costs and accelerating annual inflation suggests that businesses continue facing substantial pricing pressures despite the softer headline reading.

Data Summary — US October 2026 PPI

Indicator Oct Exp. Sep
PPI Final Demand (mom) +0.3% +0.4% +1.4%
PPI Final Demand (yoy) +6.5% +6.6% +6.3%
Final Demand Goods (mom) +0.5% +2.5%
Final Demand Services (mom) +0.2% +1.0%
PPI ex-Food, Energy & Trade Services (mom) +0.5% +0.5%
PPI ex-Food, Energy & Trade Services (yoy) +4.9%

September’s headline monthly PPI increase was revised upward from 1.3% to 1.4%.

Selected Components — October

Component Oct (mom) Sep (mom)
Final Demand Foods +1.3% +1.1%
Final Demand Energy -0.1% +10.0%
Goods ex-Food & Energy +0.5% +0.3%
Transportation & Warehousing Services +2.0% +3.4%
Trade Services -0.2% +2.1%
Processed Intermediate Goods +0.4% +2.4%
Unprocessed Intermediate Goods -3.1% +6.3%
Intermediate Services +0.6% +1.0%

Key Takeaways

  • US PPI slowed sharply from 1.4% to 0.3% mom, undershooting forecasts, but annual inflation accelerated from 6.3% to 6.5%.
  • Underlying producer inflation held at 0.5% mom, while non-energy goods and freight transportation continued recording substantial price increases.
  • Lower raw energy costs provided relief, but elevated processed input and intermediate services inflation indicated persistent pressures across production chains.

Full US PPI release here.

headline: USD/JPY Tests 160 as Modest US Intervention Commitment Raises Questions, PPI Cools Dollar
html_content:
The Central Question Is Whether Confirmed US Participation Still Provides a Meaningful Deterrent Now That Traders Know How Little Washington Actually Committed

What’s happening: USD/JPY reached 160.30 during Thursday’s New York session before retreating to around 159.89 on Friday, after a New York Fed disclosure showed that the US Treasury’s July 31 Yen purchase was only ¥79.4B (about $497M), equal to 0.5% of Japan’s ¥15.4T third-quarter intervention. Softer-than-expected US producer prices (0.3% mom against 0.4% expected) briefly interrupted the Dollar’s rally, although annual PPI accelerated to 6.5%.

Why it matters: Tokyo is trying to preserve the deterrent effect of intervention through warnings and its cooperation with the US Treasury, but a clearer view of Washington’s limited financial contribution could encourage markets to test how far Japan will act independently. With US yields and Fed tightening expectations still favoring the Dollar, a durable Yen recovery may be harder to sustain.

USD/JPY’s return above 160 has renewed scrutiny of Japan’s currency intervention strategy, particularly after a New York Fed disclosure revealed that Washington’s financial contribution to this summer’s coordinated intervention was modest compared with Tokyo’s. The pair reached 160.30 during Thursday’s New York session before retreating to around 159.89 on Friday, as softer-than-expected US producer inflation briefly interrupted the Dollar’s rally. The central question is whether confirmed US participation still provides a meaningful deterrent now that traders know how little Washington actually committed. Meanwhile, the PPI report offered some relief from the week’s hawkish Federal Reserve repricing, but persistent underlying inflation provided little reason to abandon expectations for further rate hikes.

Follow USD/JPY’s test of 160, Japan’s intervention warnings and the Dollar’s reaction to PPI on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

US Intervention Was Small, but Its Significance Goes Beyond the Amount

The New York Fed’s quarterly foreign exchange report, released Thursday, confirmed that the US Treasury purchased ¥79.4B, equivalent to approximately $497M, on July 31 by selling euros from its Exchange Stabilization Fund. The operation, conducted through the New York Fed on behalf of the Treasury, marked the first US Yen-buying intervention since 1998. The Federal Reserve itself did not intervene independently.

Japan’s Ministry of Finance, meanwhile, intervened by a total of ¥15.4T during the third quarter, following the Yen’s depreciation to around 163.99 in late July.

The US transaction amounted to just 0.5% of Japan’s quarterly intervention total, highlighting the substantial difference between Washington’s financial commitment and Tokyo’s direct market operations. Although the comparison covers different intervention periods, the scale illustrates that Japan provided the overwhelming majority of the funds used to support its currency.

US and Japanese Intervention at a Glance

  • US Treasury purchase: ¥79.4B (approximately $497M) on July 31
  • Funding: euros sold from the Exchange Stabilization Fund
  • Significance: first US Yen-buying intervention since 1998
  • Japan’s Ministry of Finance: ¥15.4T during the third quarter
  • US purchase as a share of Japan’s quarterly total: 0.5%
  • USD/JPY between July 30 and August 3: from around 164 to approximately 155

The disclosure introduces a distinction between the financial scale of intervention and the credibility created by US involvement.

Washington’s willingness to participate directly was significant. It demonstrated that US officials were prepared to move beyond verbal support and use Treasury resources to counter what they regarded as disorderly Yen movements. The coordinated operation also sent a political signal that currency stability had become a shared concern.

Yet the relatively small purchase raises questions about how much additional financial backing Japan could expect if another intervention became necessary. Traders who previously assumed coordinated action implied substantial US participation may now reassess that assumption.

The risk for Tokyo is that a clearer understanding of Washington’s limited financial contribution could encourage markets to test how far Japan is prepared to act independently.

However, the July experience also demonstrates why the dollar amount alone may underestimate the effectiveness of coordinated intervention.

Reports that the New York Fed had requested exchange-rate checks on behalf of the Treasury emerged on July 30, ahead of the actual US Yen purchase. The Yen strengthened substantially during the intervention period, with USD/JPY retreating from around 164 to approximately 155 between July 30 and August 3.

The sequence suggests that the credibility of possible joint action may have influenced expectations even before the financial operations were fully disclosed. Japan’s much larger intervention also contributed to the broader episode, making it impossible to isolate the effect of Washington’s participation.

US Participation: Signal vs Limit

What it signalled What it left in question
Washington was prepared to move beyond verbal support and use Treasury resources against disorderly Yen movements The small purchase raises questions about how much additional financial backing Japan could expect in another intervention
The coordinated operation sent a political signal that currency stability had become a shared concern Traders who assumed coordinated action implied substantial US participation may now reassess
The credibility of possible joint action may have influenced expectations before the operations were fully disclosed Japan’s much larger intervention also contributed, making it impossible to isolate the effect of Washington’s participation

The US commitment was small in financial terms, but its political and signaling value could have been considerably greater. The challenge now is whether that credibility can be sustained after the market has learned the actual size of the American purchase.

Japan Reinforces Intervention Warnings as USD/JPY Crosses 160

The disclosure comes at a sensitive moment for the Yen.

USD/JPY climbed to 160.30 during Thursday’s New York trading, crossing the psychologically important 160 threshold for the first time since early September. Although the pair subsequently retreated below the level, the move demonstrated that intervention concerns had not prevented another test.

Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama responded on Friday by warning against recent exchange-rate movements.

“We have recently seen sharp, one-sided movements in the foreign exchange market,” Katayama said, adding, “We will respond appropriately.”

She also emphasized Japan’s continued cooperation with the US Treasury, reinforcing the message that Washington remains involved in discussions surrounding currency stability.

Her comments followed Thursday’s warning from Japan’s top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura, who reminded investors of the summer intervention operations.

“It’s still too early to forget what happened this summer,” Mimura said.

Japan is attempting to preserve the deterrent effect of intervention without immediately committing to another operation.

The emphasis on US cooperation is particularly relevant following the New York Fed disclosure. Tokyo can point to actual American participation as evidence that the two countries are prepared to act together, even if Washington’s direct financial contribution was comparatively small.

Nevertheless, the previous intervention occurred after USD/JPY reached substantially higher levels than 160. That does not establish a threshold for future action, but it cautions against assuming that crossing 160 automatically triggers intervention.

Japanese officials have emphasized the speed and nature of exchange-rate movements rather than a fixed currency level. A renewed advance accompanied by rapid, one-sided depreciation could therefore provoke a different response from a more orderly move above 160.

There is also an important monetary policy dimension. Higher US Treasury yields and expectations for additional Fed tightening have supported the Dollar, while expectations for another Bank of Japan rate hike in December have not been sufficient to reverse the broader USD/JPY advance.

Japan’s ten-year government bond yield was also higher on Friday, but the continuing gap between US and Japanese monetary conditions remains relevant to the currency outlook.

Intervention can influence exchange-rate expectations and short-term positioning, but maintaining a durable Yen recovery may be harder if underlying monetary policy pressures continue favoring the Dollar.

Softer US PPI Interrupts the Dollar Rally, but Inflation Concerns Persist

The latest US inflation release provided some near-term relief for the Yen and other currencies, although the reaction was relatively contained.

US producer prices increased 0.3% mom in October, below expectations of 0.4% and sharply slower than September’s upwardly revised 1.4% increase.

The downside surprise prompted a pullback in Treasury yields and the Dollar. The US two-year yield declined from approximately 4.876% immediately before the release to a low near 4.829%, before recovering to around 4.840% by 13:40 GMT.

The Dollar Index similarly slipped from 103.187 to 103.086, subsequently recovering to approximately 103.136.

The reaction suggests that the PPI release interrupted the week’s hawkish repricing without triggering a decisive reversal.

The underlying inflation figures explain why the relief was limited.

Annual PPI inflation accelerated from 6.3% to 6.5%, its highest level since November 2022. Meanwhile, producer prices excluding food, energy and trade services increased 0.5% for the second consecutive month, with the annual rate reaching 4.9%.

The softer headline partly reflected lower energy prices and weaker trade margins, while non-energy goods and transportation costs continued showing persistent pressure.

The report therefore failed to deliver another upside surprise capable of reinforcing the Dollar’s advance, but it did not establish a broad improvement in producer inflation.

US PPI and Market Reaction at a Glance

  • Headline PPI: 0.3% mom in October, against 0.4% expected and September’s upwardly revised 1.4%
  • Annual PPI: 6.5%, up from 6.3% and the highest since November 2022
  • PPI excluding food, energy and trade services: 0.5% mom for the second consecutive month, 4.9% annually
  • US two-year yield: from approximately 4.876% to a low near 4.829%, recovering to around 4.840% by 13:40 GMT
  • Dollar Index: from 103.187 to 103.086, recovering to approximately 103.136

Fed expectations were also firmly positioned toward additional tightening before the release. CME FedWatch showed an 86.2% probability of a 25bps December hike and a 13.8% chance of 50bps, while markets assigned approximately 75% probability to at least 50bps of cumulative tightening by January.

Those probabilities were recorded shortly before PPI and do not establish how rate expectations changed afterward.

Recent Fed comments similarly reinforce the likelihood of further tightening, even as policymakers differ over the appropriate pace.

For the Dollar, the immediate question is whether the post-PPI pullback develops into a sustained adjustment or proves to be a temporary interruption of the broader tightening-driven advance.

Intervention Credibility Faces Another Test

Friday’s currency market showed a more differentiated picture than the Dollar’s earlier rally.

The Euro and Sterling were relatively firm across the major currencies, while the Swiss Franc lagged. The Dollar continued outperforming several currencies, including the Yen, but its strength was no longer uniform following the PPI release.

For USD/JPY, however, the central issue extends beyond the immediate reaction to US inflation data.

The summer intervention established that Washington was willing to participate alongside Tokyo, but the latest disclosure shows that its actual financial contribution was limited. Whether that distinction weakens the deterrent effect of coordinated action will depend on how traders respond to renewed intervention warnings and future movements in the exchange rate.

A sustained return above 160 without stronger official language or market action could encourage speculation that the threshold itself carries limited intervention significance. Conversely, more forceful warnings, renewed US involvement or actual intervention would challenge the view that the deterrent has weakened.

USD/JPY Above 160: Two Outcomes

Scenario Implication
Sustained return above 160 without stronger official language or market action Could encourage speculation that the threshold itself carries limited intervention significance
More forceful warnings, renewed US involvement or actual intervention Would challenge the view that the deterrent has weakened

The US inflation outlook also matters. If Treasury yields and the Dollar resume rising, Japan could face renewed pressure to defend the Yen despite the risks associated with intervention.

For now, USD/JPY’s break above 160 has demonstrated traders’ willingness to test the level, while the modest US intervention disclosure raises questions about how much support Tokyo can expect from Washington in another confrontation. The effectiveness of the next intervention warning may depend less on the amount previously spent than on whether markets still believe both governments are prepared to act again.

However, annual PPI inflation accelerated from 6.3% to 6.5%, its highest since November 2022, and producer prices excluding food, energy and trade services increased 0.5% for the second consecutive month. Non-energy goods prices continued rising, while freight transportation costs climbed 3.9%. The figures suggest that October’s softer headline provides relief from September’s surge, but persistent underlying and intermediate production costs offer little evidence of broad disinflation.
  • US 2-Year Yield Nears 5% as Fed Repricing Puts Silver’s 48.60 Support at Risk: The US two-year Treasury yield has surged nearly 32 basis points since Tuesday morning, approaching critical resistance between 4.96% and 5.00% as markets price further Federal Reserve tightening. Over the same period, gold and silver have each fallen approximately 5%, alongside a stronger Dollar and higher real yields. Silver’s failed recovery above 53.72 has restored its bearish near-term outlook, with another test of 48.60 favored. A decisive break could expose 46.48 and eventually 43.96, while a confirmed Treasury yield breakout above 5% could reinforce pressure on precious metals.
  • Fed’s Goolsbee Sounds Inflation Alarm as Daly and Williams Back More Tightening: Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee warned that inflation is at a “precarious moment,” with persistent services and healthcare pressures raising concerns about entrenched price increases. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly also supported further tightening but argued that rising bond yields are already restraining financial conditions, giving policymakers time to make calibrated decisions. New York Fed President John Williams reinforced the need for additional rate hikes without specifying their timing or size. Together, their comments show broad agreement that inflation requires further action, while the debate over gradual versus more aggressive tightening continues ahead of December’s policy meeting.

Eurozone and New Zealand

  • ECB’s Schnabel Warns Germany’s Export-Driven Growth Model Is No Longer Viable: ECB Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel warned that Germany’s traditional export-driven growth model is no longer viable in a fragmented global economy. Speaking in Vilnius, she argued that the country’s prolonged stagnation reflects persistent weakness in domestic consumption and investment rather than simply declining export competitiveness. German real private consumption has grown by less than 1% annually since 1999, while substantial corporate savings have flowed abroad instead of supporting domestic growth. Schnabel welcomed Germany’s major fiscal expansion, arguing that targeted public investment and structural reforms could strengthen domestic demand, raise productive capacity and create a more resilient growth model.
  • Eurozone Trade Swings to Deficit as Energy Costs Rise and EU Manufacturing Surplus Shrinks: Eurozone goods trade swung from a €13.5B surplus a year earlier to a €10.3B deficit in September, as imports surged 16.1% against export growth of 6.0%. The deterioration was driven by a wider energy deficit and a shrinking machinery and vehicles surplus. Across the EU, the trade deficit reached €16.8B, with the manufactured goods surplus falling from €32.4B to €15.8B. Trade with major partners also weakened, as the EU’s surplus with the US nearly halved and its deficit with China widened, revealing pressures extending beyond higher energy costs.
  • New Zealand BNZ Manufacturing PMI Eases to 54.9, but Broad-Based Expansion Continues: New Zealand’s BNZ–BusinessNZ PMI Manufacturing eased from 56.3 to 54.9 in October, signaling slower but continued expansion. Production declined from 56.6 to 53.9, while new orders fell from 56.8 to 54.3, pointing to softer output and demand momentum. However, all five major components stayed above the 50 expansion threshold, with employment edging higher and deliveries strengthening to 61.4. BusinessNZ also reported expansion across all manufacturing subindustries. Despite uneven regional performance and lingering political uncertainty, the figures suggest that manufacturing growth remains relatively well established, even as the pace moderates.

How much did the US contribute to the summer Yen intervention?

  7. Shortly before PPI, CME FedWatch showed 86.2% for a 25bps December hike, 13.8% for 50bps and approximately 75% for at least 50bps of cumulative tightening by January.

The immediate test is USD/JPY around 160. headline: Hawkish Fed Repricing Punishes Non-Yielders: Gold and Bitcoin Slide as Dollar Surges to 2026 High
html_content:
TL;DR: Last week’s hawkish Fed repricing, not a flight from risk, drove yields and the Dollar higher and hit non-yielding gold and Bitcoin, while equities rose and volatility fell. Markets have now priced far more tightening than any Fed official has endorsed, so the 5% test in the two-year yield and whether the Fed validates that path are the next questions.

Why Did Hawkish Fed Repricing Hit Gold and Bitcoin While Stocks Rose?

Financial markets underwent a substantial hawkish reassessment of Federal Reserve policy last week, driving US Treasury yields sharply higher and pushing Dollar Index to a new 2026 high. Gold and Bitcoin suffered heavy losses as tighter financial conditions increased pressure on assets that offer no conventional interest income. Yet US equities advanced and market volatility declined, suggesting that the dominant force was a repricing of interest rate expectations rather than a broad flight from risk.

The scale of the adjustment was striking. Markets entered the week pricing roughly two additional quarter-point Fed hikes through 2027, but ended it anticipating nearly four. The shift was triggered by Fed Governor Christopher Waller’s warning that larger increases might be necessary, followed by an October CPI report that met his threshold for considering a 50bps move. Other policymakers reinforced the need for further tightening, although they differed over its pace and offered no clear endorsement of the full path markets had priced.

The key question for the coming week is whether the Fed can justify the additional tightening already embedded in market prices. The technical picture adds urgency: US two-year yields are approaching 5%, Dollar Index has broken above significant resistance, gold is threatening a decisive breakdown below 3,870, and Bitcoin has already breached a major retracement level.

Follow the Fed repricing and its impact on gold, Bitcoin and the Dollar on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

Fed Expectations Shift From Two Hikes to Nearly Four

The most consequential change was not the expectation of another December rate increase. Markets had already assigned a 76.3% probability to a hike before the week began, with further tightening anticipated during 2027.

What changed was the expected scale and timing of those increases.

At the November 6 close of the previous trading week, Fed funds pricing implied approximately 47bps of additional tightening through September 2027, equivalent to just under two quarter-point hikes. By Friday, November 13, that expectation had climbed to around 90bps, or approximately 3.6 hikes.

Markets had almost doubled the amount of additional tightening they expected the Fed to deliver.

The December 8–9 meeting moved from a 76.3% probability of a hike to a fully priced increase, with CME FedWatch assigning 88.5% to a 25bps move and 11.5% to 50bps. More significantly, the probability of at least 50bps of cumulative tightening by January jumped from 15.8% to 76.6%.

The repricing extended progressively further along the policy horizon. Expected cumulative tightening for December increased by approximately 9bps, while the September 2027 expectation rose by 43bps.

  • Cumulative tightening through September 2027: about 47bps (Nov 6) to about 90bps (Nov 13)
  • December hike: 76.3% probability to fully priced (88.5% for 25bps, 11.5% for 50bps)
  • At least 50bps of cumulative tightening by January: 15.8% to 76.6%

That distinction is critical. The market was not simply betting on a larger December hike. It was pricing a more sustained tightening cycle and a higher eventual policy rate.

The adjustment was largely completed by early Thursday. Subsequent changes through Friday were relatively modest, indicating that the strongest phase of repricing had already occurred before the week’s final inflation release.

Friday’s expected tightening path also raises a question about market positioning. With almost 90bps of additional increases priced through September 2027, further hawkish surprises would need to justify either a faster sequence of hikes or a higher eventual policy peak.

Waller’s Warning and October CPI Triggered the Repricing

The turning point came on Tuesday, November 10, when Fed Governor Christopher Waller raised the possibility of accelerating monetary tightening.

Speaking at the Bank of England Watchers Conference in London ahead of the US inflation release, Waller supported a 25bps December increase even if inflation improved from September. However, he argued that a 50bps move should be considered if monthly core CPI reached approximately 0.3% or higher.

“Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk,” Waller warned.

The concern was not confined to the immediate inflation figures. Waller argued that expected future rate increases had already tightened financial conditions. If the Fed failed to deliver the tightening markets anticipated, interest rates could fall and financial conditions could loosen, undermining efforts to restore price stability.

His argument introduced a feedback mechanism between Fed policy and market expectations: financial markets were already delivering restraint that policymakers might need to preserve.

October CPI subsequently reinforced that concern.

Core consumer prices increased 0.3% mom for a third consecutive month, exceeding expectations of 0.2% and meeting the threshold Waller had identified. Headline CPI rose 0.4%, also above the 0.3% forecast, although it slowed from September’s 0.6% increase.

The internal details were mixed. Shelter inflation moderated, and core goods inflation eased slightly. However, services excluding rent of shelter accelerated from 0.3% to 0.5% mom, suggesting persistent price pressure beyond the most volatile components.

The combination of Waller’s conditional warning and the subsequent inflation surprise gave investors a concrete reason to reassess the Fed’s policy trajectory.

The Treasury market responded immediately, with the two-year yield rising sharply on Tuesday. Additional pressure developed later in the week as investors absorbed the implications of persistent inflation and further Fed commentary.

Friday’s PPI release provided a modest counterweight. Headline producer prices increased 0.3% against expectations of 0.4%, prompting some retreat in yields and the Dollar. Yet underlying PPI excluding food, energy and trade services held at 0.5% for a second month, while annual headline producer inflation reached 6.5%.

The PPI downside surprise interrupted the advance but did not materially challenge the broader inflation concerns that had driven the week’s repricing.

Fed Officials Support More Tightening, but Differ Over Pace

Waller’s comments were the clearest catalyst for a more aggressive interpretation of Fed policy, but the wider message from policymakers was more nuanced.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan supported at least two additional quarter-point increases, stating that the FOMC needed to implement “at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases.” She also suggested that faster action might become appropriate.

Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid described policy as “fairly accommodative,” reinforcing the argument that interest rates had not yet reached a sufficiently restrictive setting.

Others shared concerns about inflation without endorsing larger immediate increases.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favored smaller, more frequent hikes, arguing that gradual tightening would allow households and businesses to adjust more smoothly. Despite acknowledging that inflation was moving in the wrong direction, she rejected the idea that the Fed had fallen sufficiently behind to require more aggressive action.

“I don’t think we’re behind the curve today,” Hammack said.

San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly also expected further tightening but emphasized that rising Treasury yields were already contributing to tighter financial conditions. She described higher yields as “most welcome,” arguing that market-driven restraint gave the Fed additional time to make calibrated decisions.

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee warned that inflation was at a “precarious moment,” particularly as services price pressures persisted beyond tariffs and energy. New York Fed President John Williams similarly supported further tightening without specifying its timing or magnitude.

Comments from Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson and Boston Fed President Susan Collins also favored measured increases, while leaving room for faster action if inflation developments warranted it.

The emerging consensus is that rates need to rise further. The disagreement concerns how quickly the Fed must act, and how much additional tightening will ultimately be necessary.

This distinction leaves a potentially important gap between market expectations and policymakers’ expressed intentions.

That does not mean the market is necessarily overpricing the cycle. Persistent inflation could eventually validate the projected path. However, the current level of market expectations requires stronger confirmation than a general agreement among policymakers that further hikes are necessary.

Treasury Yields Lead Dollar Higher While Equities Resist Risk-Off Pressure

The Treasury market delivered the clearest expression of the policy adjustment.

The US two-year yield surged 34bps during the week, from 4.512% to 4.852%. The ten-year yield increased 28bps to 5.139%, while the thirty-year yield rose approximately 21bps.

The larger increase at the front end narrowed the spread between two-year and ten-year yields from approximately 34.7bps to 28.7bps.

  • US two-year yield: +34bps, 4.512% to 4.852%
  • US ten-year yield: +28bps to 5.139%
  • US thirty-year yield: about +21bps
  • Two-year/ten-year spread: about 34.7bps to 28.7bps

That flattening is consistent with a repricing driven primarily by expected Fed policy rather than a rise in longer-term borrowing costs alone.

Bond yields also increased in Germany, Britain, Canada and Japan, but the US moves were larger. The resulting widening in yield differentials provided a fundamental basis for the Dollar’s advance.

Dollar Index climbed 1.11% over the week to close at 103.410, breaking above its previous 2026 high around 102.945. The weekly FX heat map showed broad Dollar strength against all seven major counterparts, although the Yen and New Zealand Dollar held up relatively well while Swiss Franc was particularly weak.

The nature of the Dollar rally is important.

The evidence points more strongly toward a yield-differential advance than a conventional safe-haven bid. Swiss Franc weakness and falling equity-market volatility contrast with what would normally accompany broad defensive positioning.

Indeed, US stocks recovered despite the sharp rise in yields.

S&P 500 gained approximately 2.5% for the week, Nasdaq advanced 2.3%, and Dow Jones rose 2.1%. VIX declined by about 25%, reflecting a substantial reduction in the market stress seen during the preceding week.

  • Dollar Index: +1.11% to 103.410 (previous 2026 high around 102.945)
  • S&P 500: about +2.5%; Nasdaq: +2.3%; Dow Jones: +2.1%
  • VIX: down about 25%

Part of the equity recovery therefore reflected relief from earlier selling. Higher yields nevertheless continued to challenge valuations, particularly in longer-duration technology shares. Nasdaq finished Friday lower even as the major indices retained positive weekly performances.

The result was a differentiated market response rather than a uniform withdrawal from risk.

Gold and Bitcoin Bear the Brunt of Tighter Financial Conditions

The impact of higher yields and Dollar strength was considerably more pronounced in gold and Bitcoin.

Gold fell 4.56% during the week to close at 3,883.94, while Bitcoin declined approximately 9.93% on its weekly chart, trading around 67,300 during Saturday’s snapshot. Silver also suffered substantial losses.

Immediate focus is now on the 4.960–5.000% resistance zone.

The weekly chart highlights the potential scale of that correction.

The critical distinction is that gold has tested support without confirming a sustained breakdown. The technical outlook favors further weakness, but confirmation of the next downward leg is still required.

headline: Fed’s Inflation Fight Shifts to Pace as Schmid Rejects Excuses, Collins Backs Gradual Hikes
html_content:
Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid argued Sunday that persistent inflation cannot be dismissed as the unavoidable consequence of supply shocks or demand that is resistant to monetary tightening. Speaking at a credit union conference in Hawaii, Schmid said inflation was “uncomfortably above the 2% price stability target, and moving in the wrong direction.” He rejected arguments that supply disruptions or AI-related investment demand limit the Fed’s ability to restore price stability, emphasizing that inflation ultimately reflects an imbalance between supply and demand. “The Fed does have the tools to address inflation and has the responsibility to achieve price stability,” he said. However, Schmid stopped short of explicitly calling for additional rate hikes.

Boston Fed President Susan Collins, speaking Saturday at a housing conference in Boston, supported further tightening but favored a measured approach. “A steady, gradual path seems appropriate to me at the moment. But I’m open-minded,” she told reporters. Collins acknowledged that stronger inflation readings over the past three months and a firmer labor market had raised her expectations for the policy rate path over the coming year. However, she cautioned that higher medium- and longer-term interest rates could already be restraining demand more than anticipated, while additional economic shocks remained a risk. She also stressed that gradual tightening did not imply a predetermined pace of rate increases.

The remarks reinforce the Fed’s tightening bias while highlighting a developing debate over the appropriate pace of further rate increases. Schmid’s argument challenges the notion that persistent inflation lies beyond the Fed’s control, while Collins emphasizes the need to balance inflation risks against the economic effects of tighter financial conditions. With interest rate futures fully pricing a 25bps hike in December and assigning a small probability to a 50bps increase, the distinction is increasingly relevant. Both officials support the case for restoring price stability, but neither endorsed the more aggressive tightening path currently contemplated by markets.

Key Takeaways

  • Schmid rejects inflation excuses: Supply shocks and AI-driven demand do not place persistent inflation beyond the Fed’s ability to control.
  • Collins supports gradual tightening: Stronger inflation and labor data justify a higher policy rate path, but rising market yields may already restrain demand.
  • The debate shifts toward pace: Both officials reinforce the case for tighter policy without explicitly endorsing the aggressive rate path priced by markets.

Collins acknowledged that stronger inflation readings over the past three months and a firmer labor market had raised her expectations for the policy rate path over the coming year. However, she cautioned that higher medium- and longer-term interest rates could already be restraining demand more than anticipated, while additional economic shocks remained a risk. She also stressed that gradual tightening did not imply a predetermined pace of rate increases. The remarks reinforce the Fed’s tightening bias while highlighting a developing debate over the appropriate pace of further rate increases. Schmid’s argument challenges the notion that persistent inflation lies beyond the Fed’s control, while Collins emphasizes the need to balance inflation risks against the economic effects of tighter financial conditions. With interest rate futures fully pricing a 25bps hike in December and assigning a small probability to a 50bps increase, the distinction is increasingly relevant. Both officials support the case for restoring price stability, but neither endorsed the more aggressive tightening path currently contemplated by markets. Key Takeaways Schmid rejects inflation excuses: Supply shocks and AI-driven demand do not place persistent inflation beyond the Fed’s ability to control. Collins supports gradual tightening: Stronger inflation and labor data justify a higher policy rate path, but rising market yields may already restrain demand. The debate shifts toward pace: Both officials reinforce the case for tighter policy without explicitly endorsing the aggressive rate path priced by markets.

headline: NZ BNZ Services Hits Highest Since 2023 as Stronger Activity Outpaces Hiring
html_content:
New Zealand’s BNZ–BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index (PSI) rose from 50.9 in September to 51.7 in October, reaching its highest level since 2023 and signaling a further strengthening in services activity. The improvement was driven primarily by Activity/Sales, which climbed from 50.4 to 52.6, while New Orders/Business increased from 52.5 to 53.0. The stronger activity reading suggests that earlier gains in new orders are beginning to translate into actual business activity, providing encouraging evidence that the services expansion is gaining traction following a prolonged period of weakness.

However, the improvement has yet to translate into meaningful employment growth. The Employment subindex edged up from 49.8 to 49.9, remaining just below the 50 expansion threshold and pointing to broadly stagnant hiring. Weakness also persisted in discretionary consumer services, with cultural, recreational and personal activities under pressure, while retail trade remained subdued despite October’s school holidays. These divergences suggest that the recovery in services demand is still uneven, with businesses experiencing stronger activity without a corresponding improvement in staffing or consumer-facing sectors.

The broader economic picture was also more constructive. The GDP-weighted BNZ–BusinessNZ Performance of Composite Index (PCI), combining manufacturing and services, rose from 51.5 to 52.2, while the free-weighted measure edged up from 53.3 to 53.4. Both manufacturing and services components remained in expansion territory, indicating that improving services activity is contributing to a wider pickup in business conditions. Nevertheless, the contrast between stronger activity and stagnant employment suggests that the expansion is not yet translating into broad-based economic momentum.

headline: Japan GDP Contracts as Consumer Spending Falters, Business Investment Offers Rare Bright Spot
html_content:
Japan’s economy contracted for the first time in four quarters, as weak household consumption and a sharp deterioration in net exports outweighed stronger business investment. Real GDP growth slowed from an annualized 1.4% in Q2 to -0.1% in Q3, missing market expectations of 0.3% growth. On a quarterly basis, GDP edged down 0.02%. Private consumption, accounting for more than half of economic activity, fell 0.3% for a second consecutive quarter, weighed down by elevated living costs and adverse weather, including heavy rainfall and July’s Kumamoto earthquake. Household spending on durable goods reversed sharply from 3.6% growth to a 3.5% contraction, while services consumption managed only a marginal 0.1% increase.

External trade was another major drag, with net exports subtracting 0.6 percentage point from quarterly GDP growth, reversing a positive 0.6-point contribution in Q2. Total exports shifted from 1.6% growth to a 0.2% decline, while imports rebounded from a 1.3% contraction to a 2.5% increase. Beneath the headline, goods exports rose 2.4%, but services exports plunged 7.1%, while goods imports increased 3.9%. Business investment provided a notable counterweight, rising 1.6% after a 0.4% decline in Q2, supported by spending on labor-saving equipment, digitalization and AI-related technologies. However, residential investment fell 1.1%, highlighting continued weakness in other parts of domestic demand.

The underlying picture was weaker than the marginal GDP contraction suggested. Final sales of domestic product, which exclude inventory changes, fell 0.5% qoq, equivalent to a 2.1% annualized decline. Domestic demand contributed 0.6 percentage point to growth, offsetting the negative contribution from net exports, but this included a substantial 0.5-point contribution from public inventory changes rather than stronger final demand. The divergence between resilient corporate investment and struggling household consumption underscores the uneven state of Japan’s economy. While temporary weather disruptions contributed to the weakness, persistent pressure on household purchasing power raises questions about the sustainability of domestic demand, complicating the BoJ’s assessment of further monetary tightening.

  • Japan’s economy contracts: Real GDP shifted from 1.4% annualized growth to a 0.1% contraction, missing expectations as consumption and net exports weakened.
  • Business investment offers resilience: Corporate capital spending rebounded 1.6%, supported by automation, digitalization and AI demand, while household spending contracted again.

headline: China Industrial Output Slows to 4.8%, Retail Sales Growth Falls to 0.4%
html_content:
China’s economic momentum weakened further in October, with industrial production, retail sales and fixed-asset investment all missing market expectations. Industrial output growth slowed from 5.5% to 4.8% yoy, below the 5.3% forecast, while retail sales growth decelerated from 1.1% to just 0.4%, missing expectations of 0.8%. Fixed-asset investment contracted 8.1% yoy over January–October, deepening from the 7.2% decline recorded in the first nine months and falling short of expectations for a 7.0% contraction. The simultaneous disappointments highlight persistent weakness in domestic demand, even as export-oriented and technology-intensive industries continue to provide support to the economy.

Industrial performance remained highly uneven. High-tech manufacturing expanded 17.6% yoy, while equipment manufacturing grew 10.6%, substantially outperforming overall industrial production. Output of 3D printing devices, lithium-ion batteries and industrial robots surged 85.9%, 30.0% and 26.0%, respectively. However, this strength contrasted with subdued household spending. Goods retail sales increased just 0.3% yoy in October, while catering revenue rose 0.7%. Services consumption offered some resilience, with retail sales of services growing 4.9% over January–October, compared with 0.9% for goods under the broader retail measure. The divergence underscores how strength in advanced manufacturing has yet to translate into a meaningful improvement in domestic consumption.

Investment weakness added to concerns about the sustainability of growth. Real estate development investment plunged 21.6% yoy over January–October, but the downturn extended well beyond property, with investment excluding real estate falling 5.1%, manufacturing investment declining 2.9% and infrastructure investment dropping 5.1%. Private investment contracted 11.4%, despite continued growth in selected high-tech sectors. Meanwhile, October goods exports surged 28.7% yoy in yuan terms, demonstrating the continued importance of external demand. The National Bureau of Statistics acknowledged that the imbalance between strong supply and weak demand remained acute. With domestic spending and investment failing to match the strength of technology-driven production and exports, China’s growth outlook remains heavily dependent on external demand and a narrower group of high-performing industries.

  • Investment weakness extends beyond property: Falling manufacturing, infrastructure and private investment highlight domestic fragility despite strong exports and technology-driven production.

headline: Canada CPI Today, UK CPI Wednesday: Can Inflation Finally Break GBP/CAD’s Range?
html_content:
TL;DR: GBP/CAD faces back-to-back inflation tests, Canada CPI today and UK CPI on Wednesday, after both central banks resumed hiking without giving the cross a direction. With broadly parallel rate paths priced, only a surprise large enough to shift one side’s policy outlook relative to the other’s is likely to break the 1.8604–1.9042 range.

Why Are Rate Hikes Not Moving GBP/CAD Out of Its Range?

GBP/CAD faces two important inflation tests this week after the Bank of Canada and Bank of England both resumed raising interest rates, yet neither move was enough to establish a decisive direction for the cross. BoC raised its overnight rate by 25bps to 2.50% on October 28, followed by BoE’s 25bps increase to 4.00% on November 5. Despite the tightening on both sides, GBP/CAD has remained confined to a broad consolidation between 1.8604 and 1.9042, trading around 1.8851 in early Monday trading.

Canada’s October CPI, due today at 13:30 GMT, and the UK’s inflation report on Wednesday at 07:00 GMT will test whether broadly synchronized policy expectations can finally diverge enough to break that range.

Follow today’s Canada CPI release and Wednesday’s UK CPI reaction on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

Canada CPI: Greater Scope for Near-Term BoC Repricing

The immediate focus is Canada, where markets have greater room to reassess the near-term tightening outlook. OIS pricing indicates approximately 13.4bps of additional tightening by the December 9 BoC meeting, followed by 29.6bps by January 27 and 43.6bps by March 3. By October 2027, the curve implies 78.7bps of cumulative additional increases, equivalent to slightly more than three quarter-point hikes.

  • December 9: about 13.4bps of additional tightening priced
  • January 27: about 29.6bps
  • March 3: about 43.6bps
  • October 2027: about 78.7bps (slightly more than three quarter-point hikes)

These expectations leave the December decision relatively open, making today’s inflation figures particularly important. Headline CPI accelerated from 3.0% to 3.1% yoy in September, while the median and trimmed-mean measures stood at 1.9% and 1.8%, respectively. October headline inflation is expected to rise to 3.2%, with CPI median projected at 2.0%.

A stronger-than-expected reading, particularly in underlying inflation, could reinforce expectations of another December hike and support CAD. Conversely, softer inflation could prompt markets to reduce near-term tightening expectations, weighing on the Canadian currency.

UK CPI: December Largely Priced, 2027 Path at Stake

The UK’s inflation outlook presents a different challenge for market pricing. September headline CPI accelerated from 3.1% to 3.5% yoy, while core inflation increased from 2.6% to 2.8% and services inflation rose from 3.4% to 3.7%. October headline CPI is expected to reach 3.6%, with core inflation projected at 2.8%.

OIS markets already imply approximately 19.5bps of tightening at the December 17 BoE meeting, equivalent to a 78% probability of a 25bps increase under a simple binary assumption. Cumulative tightening expectations rise to 37.7bps by February, 53.3bps by March and 91.2bps by November 2027, implying a policy rate near 4.91%.

  • December 17: about 19.5bps (about 78% probability of a 25bps hike)
  • February: about 37.7bps
  • March: about 53.3bps
  • November 2027: about 91.2bps (policy rate near 4.91%)

With a December increase substantially priced, Wednesday’s inflation report may have greater significance for the expected extent of tightening through 2027 than for the immediate decision alone. A persistent acceleration in underlying inflation could validate the current rate path or encourage further repricing, while softer readings would challenge expectations for nearly four additional quarter-point increases.

Parallel OIS Paths Keep GBP/CAD in Balance

The comparison between the two OIS curves helps explain GBP/CAD’s lack of a sustained directional move. Markets currently price 91.2bps of additional BoE tightening over approximately the coming year, against 78.7bps for BoC, leaving a relatively modest 12.5bps difference between the cumulative increases at the final compared meetings.

Both curves have also shifted higher over the past week, limiting the change in the relative monetary policy outlook. The UK advantage is somewhat larger at several intermediate meetings, but neither currency enjoys an overwhelming advantage from incremental rate expectations.

Consequently, the critical issue is not simply whether inflation exceeds forecasts, but whether one country’s data generates a substantially larger policy repricing than the other’s.

Two CPI Releases, Two Routes Out of the Range

The sequence of releases creates an asymmetric opportunity. Canada’s CPI arrives first, with greater scope to alter the pricing of its December decision. A downside surprise could weaken CAD and push GBP/CAD toward the upper boundary of its consolidation before Wednesday’s UK CPI. If British inflation then exceeds expectations, the combined repricing could provide the catalyst for an upside breakout.

Conversely, stronger Canadian inflation followed by softer UK figures would favor a decline toward range support. UK labour data on Tuesday and retail sales releases from both countries on Friday provide additional evidence on domestic economic conditions.

However, with both central banks already expected to tighten further, modest surprises may generate volatility without establishing a lasting directional trend. A decisive breakout would likely require a meaningful change in the relative policy outlook rather than an isolated inflation surprise.

ActionForex’s Technical View: GBP/CAD, Consolidation Within a Larger Uptrend

Daily Outlook: 1.8795 EMA Holds the Near-Term Key

GBP/CAD continues to consolidate after reaching 1.9042 in July. The decline from that high to 1.8604 is viewed as the first leg of the consolidation, with the subsequent rise forming the second leg.

A sustained break below the 55-day EMA, currently around 1.8795, would suggest that the third leg has begun, opening another decline toward the 38.2% retracement of 1.8017 to 1.9042 at 1.8650. Strong support around 1.8604 should contain the downside under this scenario.

On the upside, a break above 1.8995 would bring another test of 1.9042. A decisive break through that resistance would invalidate the current consolidation interpretation and signal resumption of the larger uptrend.

From the early Monday level of 1.8851, the upper boundary is approximately 191 pips away, compared with 247 pips to 1.8604. Nevertheless, the proximity of the 55-day EMA means a relatively modest inflation surprise could trigger an important short-term move without necessarily breaking the broader range.

Weekly Outlook: Bullish Structure Favors Eventual Upside Break

The longer-term outlook remains constructive, with the uptrend from the 2022 low at 1.4069 intact within a rising channel. The 55-week EMA, currently near 1.8664, provides additional support around the 1.8604–1.8650 zone, reinforcing the view that the current consolidation is corrective within the larger advance.

An eventual upside breakout remains favored, with the 61.8% projection of 1.6355 to 1.8912 from 1.8017 targeting 1.9597.

However, a decisive break below the 1.8604–1.8650 support zone, accompanied by sustained trading beneath the 55-week EMA, would raise the possibility that the entire uptrend from 1.4069 is undergoing a larger correction, potentially exposing 1.8017.

For now, Canada’s inflation release has greater potential to reshape immediate rate expectations, while the UK figures will determine whether the relative tightening outlook shifts further in Sterling’s favor. A sustained GBP/CAD breakout will likely require more than a temporary inflation surprise: it will need a meaningful divergence in the policy paths priced for the two central banks.

Key Takeaways

  • GBP/CAD has stayed in a 1.8604–1.9042 range, trading around 1.8851, despite BoC (2.50%) and BoE (4.00%) hikes.
  • Canada’s October CPI (13:30 GMT today) has greater scope to change near-term pricing, with about 13.4bps of BoC tightening priced for December 9 and 78.7bps by October 2027.
  • UK CPI (Wednesday, 07:00 GMT) matters more for the 2027 path, since December is largely priced (about 78%) and 91.2bps is priced by November 2027.
  • The 12.5bps gap between the two cumulative paths is modest, so a breakout needs a relative repricing rather than an isolated surprise.
  • Support lies at the 55-day EMA near 1.8795, then 1.8650 and 1.8604, while resistance is 1.8995 and 1.9042, with 1.9597 the larger upside target.

Stay ahead of Canada and UK CPI and the next move in GBP/CAD—join the ActionForex Telegram channel for regular market updates and analysis.

By October 2027, the curve implies 78.7bps of cumulative additional increases, equivalent to slightly more than three quarter-point hikes. December 9: about 13.4bps of additional tightening priced January 27: about 29.6bps March 3: about 43.6bps October 2027: about 78.7bps (slightly more than three quarter-point hikes) These expectations leave the December decision relatively open, making today’s inflation figures particularly important. Headline CPI accelerated from 3.0% to 3.1% yoy in September, while the median and trimmed-mean measures stood at 1.9% and 1.8%, respectively. October headline inflation is expected to rise to 3.2%, with CPI median projected at 2.0%. A stronger-than-expected reading, particularly in underlying inflation, could reinforce expectations of another December hike and support CAD. Conversely, softer inflation could prompt markets to reduce near-term tightening expectations, weighing on the Canadian currency. UK CPI: December Largely Priced, 2027 Path at Stake The UK’s inflation outlook presents a different challenge for market pricing. September headline CPI accelerated from 3.1% to 3.5% yoy, while core inflation increased from 2.6% to 2.8% and services inflation rose from 3.4% to 3.7%. October headline CPI is expected to reach 3.6%, with core inflation projected at 2.8%. OIS markets already imply approximately 19.5bps of tightening at the December 17 BoE meeting, equivalent to a 78% probability of a 25bps increase under a simple binary assumption. A persistent acceleration in underlying inflation could validate the current rate path or encourage further repricing, while softer readings would challenge expectations for nearly four additional quarter-point increases. Markets currently price 91.2bps of additional BoE tightening over approximately the coming year, against 78.7bps for BoC, leaving a relatively modest 12.5bps difference between the cumulative increases at the final compared meetings. Both curves have also shifted higher over the past week, limiting the change in the relative monetary policy outlook. The UK advantage is somewhat larger at several intermediate meetings, but neither currency enjoys an overwhelming advantage from incremental rate expectations. Consequently, the critical issue is not simply whether inflation exceeds forecasts, but whether one country’s data generates a substantially larger policy repricing than the other’s. If British inflation then exceeds expectations, the combined repricing could provide the catalyst for an upside breakout. Conversely, stronger Canadian inflation followed by softer UK figures would favor a decline toward range support. UK labour data on Tuesday and retail sales releases from both countries on Friday provide additional evidence on domestic economic conditions. headline: BoJ’s Takata Urges Faster Rate Hikes as Weak Yen and Low Real Rates Threaten Inflation
html_content:
BoJ board member Hajime Takata called for a more nimble approach to monetary tightening, arguing that Japan has entered a new policy phase in which preventing an inflation overshoot should take priority over encouraging underlying price growth. Speaking at a meeting of the Tokushima Association of Corporate Executives on Monday, Takata said 2026 requires a “regime change,” moving away from the relatively fixed pace of rate increases seen in 2024–2025. He argued that the BoJ “needs to take nimble and data-dependent actions” in response to economic and inflation developments. Takata reiterated that he had proposed raising the policy rate from 1.25% to 1.50% at October’s meeting, reflecting his preference for earlier tightening. With underlying inflation having effectively reached the 2% target, he said the central bank must shift from encouraging higher inflation toward demonstrating its determination to prevent prices from overshooting.

Takata also urged the BoJ to move its policy rate toward a “good” position near the midpoint of its estimated neutral rate range of 1.1%–2.5%, equivalent to approximately 1.8%. Such positioning would give policymakers greater flexibility to respond to future economic and inflation shocks through either hikes or cuts. He emphasized that Japan’s real policy rate remains exceptionally low compared with other major economies, leaving monetary conditions accommodative and potentially contributing to Yen weakness and higher import costs. With firms increasingly willing to pass rising costs into selling prices, exchange-rate depreciation could amplify inflation pressures. Takata also warned that Japan’s neutral interest rate could exceed current market expectations as overseas central banks tighten, reinforcing his argument that policy adjustments should not be constrained by predetermined intervals or rate ranges.

Supporting his case for faster normalization, Takata pointed to resilient corporate earnings, stronger balance sheets and sustained AI-related investment demand, arguing that the cumulative restraining effects of previous rate hikes were still some way off. Despite early-November equity market turbulence, he said, “I believe AI investment will remain solid overall.” However, his assessment contrasts with Japan’s latest GDP figures, which showed a marginal 0.1% annualized contraction in Q3, alongside a 0.3% decline in private consumption and a sharper 2.1% annualized fall in final sales of domestic product. Business investment nevertheless rose 1.6%, lending support to his confidence in corporate resilience. Takata’s remarks strengthen the hawkish argument for another rate increase as soon as December, although they represent his personal policy position rather than a commitment by the broader board. Governor Kazuo Ueda’s November 30 speech and news conference will provide the next opportunity to assess whether that preference is gaining wider support.

Key Takeaways

  • Takata calls for faster tightening: The BoJ board member urges a policy regime change, shifting from encouraging inflation toward preventing an overshoot of the 2% target.
  • Low real rates threaten Yen stability: Takata favors moving rates closer to neutral, warning that exceptionally accommodative conditions could weaken the Yen and amplify imported inflation.
  • Corporate resilience supports hikes despite weak GDP: Strong balance sheets and AI investment underpin his hawkish stance, even as Japan’s economy contracted in Q3.

Full speech of BoJ’s Takata here.

headline: Silver Sinks Toward $42 as Risk Aversion Adds to Dollar and Yield Pressure
html_content:
TL;DR: Silver is sliding faster than gold as risk aversion in equities adds to existing Dollar and yield pressure, and the gold/silver ratio breakout confirms its relative downtrend. With $46.48 support the level guarding the path toward $42, US equities and Nvidia’s earnings will show whether risk sentiment keeps driving the selloff.

Why Is Silver Falling Faster Than Gold Today?

Silver extended its selloff today so far, falling 2.78% to around $47.34 and deepening its underperformance against gold as weakness across Asian equity markets added to pressure on precious metals. Gold declined a comparatively modest 0.70%, while platinum lost 1.06% and copper slipped 0.63%. Silver’s losses followed a 6.18% decline last week, compared with gold’s 4.56% fall, highlighting its greater vulnerability to the deterioration in market sentiment. The gold/silver ratio surged another 2.20% to 81.425, breaking above its previous high at 80.110 and confirming renewed momentum in silver’s relative downtrend.

Risk Aversion Adds to Existing Dollar and Yield Pressure

Monday’s selling showed a different pattern from the previous week’s broad repricing of financial conditions. Asian equities came under substantial pressure, with Nikkei 225 dropping 2.42% and South Korea’s KOSPI losing 3.59%, amid renewed turbulence in technology and semiconductor shares. Silver’s decline was more than three times as large as gold’s, suggesting that the metal was behaving increasingly like a high-beta risk asset rather than a defensive precious metal. Gold itself attracted little haven demand, also trading lower.

Importantly, the additional weakness in silver occurred without a corresponding rise in Treasury yields or the Dollar. DXY was virtually unchanged around 103.41, while the US two-year and 10-year yields hovered near 4.855% and 5.137%, respectively, little changed from Friday’s closes. This contrasts with last week’s substantial tightening in financial conditions, when two-year yields surged 34bps, 10-year yields rose 28bps and the Dollar reached a 2026 high. Those developments increased the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding metals and established the broader bearish backdrop, as discussed in our earlier report, Hawkish Fed Repricing Punishes Non-Yielders: Gold and Bitcoin Slide as Dollar Surges to 2026 High.

  • Nikkei 225: −2.42%; KOSPI: −3.59%
  • DXY: virtually unchanged around 103.41
  • US two-year yield: near 4.855%; 10-year yield: near 5.137% (little changed from Friday)
  • Last week: two-year yield +34bps, 10-year yield +28bps, Dollar at a 2026 high

The distinction suggests that while higher yields and Dollar strength have been weighing on precious metals, Monday’s disproportionate silver losses were more closely associated with broader risk aversion. That interpretation is consistent with the observed cross-asset movements, although direct evidence of selling flows is unavailable.

Follow silver’s slide toward $42 and the risk-sentiment signals behind it on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

Gold/Silver Ratio, Breakout Reinforces Silver’s Underperformance

The gold/silver ratio provides further evidence of silver’s relative weakness. Its rebound from 76.299 has extended through 80.110, confirming resumption of the uptrend. The next target is the 100% projection of 52.720 to 72.554 from 64.647, at 84.481.

The ratio’s rise is particularly significant because gold has also been declining. It reflects silver losing value faster than gold, rather than investors actively bidding up gold. Further deterioration in equity markets could reinforce this divergence and push the ratio toward 84.481, although elevated daily and four-hour RSI readings suggest that some consolidation may occur along the way. The near-term bullish outlook for the ratio remains intact as long as 76.299 support holds.

US Equities and Nvidia Results Provide the Next Tests

The upcoming US equity session will provide an immediate test of whether silver’s underperformance is primarily reflecting broader risk sentiment. Continued weakness in Nasdaq alongside further silver losses, particularly if Treasury yields and the Dollar remain stable, would strengthen the high-beta interpretation. Conversely, a recovery in equities accompanied by silver stabilization could suggest that the latest phase of selling is easing.

Attention will also turn to Nvidia’s earnings release on Tuesday after the US market close, following recent turbulence in technology shares. The reaction in US equities and Asian semiconductor stocks could help determine whether risk aversion persists. A relief rally accompanied by silver outperforming gold would support the view that broader risk sentiment has been an important driver of the metal’s recent weakness. However, if equities recover while silver continues to decline, the influence of the existing Dollar and yield backdrop would warrant greater attention.

ActionForex’s Technical View: Silver, $46.48 Support Guards the Path to $42

Four-Hour Outlook: Downtrend Intact Despite Oversold Conditions

Silver’s selloff continues without a clear indication of bottoming. With the four-hour RSI falling to around 21, deeply oversold conditions could provide some temporary support near the 38.2% projection of 67.54 to 48.60 from 53.72, at 46.48.

Nevertheless, a decisive break below 46.48 would indicate renewed downside acceleration and open the way toward the 61.8% projection at 42.01.

On the upside, a break above 49.67 minor resistance would bring some consolidation first, but the near-term outlook will stay bearish as long as 53.72 resistance holds.

Daily Outlook: Larger Decline from $121.64 Still Unfolding

The medium-term downtrend from the record high at 121.64 remains firmly in progress. Last week’s close below the 61.8% projection of 89.36 to 54.77 from 71.16, at 49.77, followed by Monday’s additional losses, indicates persistent downward momentum. The next medium-term projection target stands at 36.56.

A sustained break above 54.77, now turned resistance, is needed to provide an initial indication of bottoming. Otherwise, the broader outlook remains bearish, with any near-term rebound more likely to represent consolidation within the existing decline.

For now, the combination of elevated Treasury yields, a strong Dollar and deteriorating risk sentiment continues to weigh on silver. The breakout in the gold/silver ratio reinforces the prospect of further underperformance. While oversold conditions could interrupt the decline, a decisive break below 46.48 would strengthen the case for an extension toward 42.01, particularly if equity-market weakness persists.

Key Takeaways

  • Silver fell 2.78% to around $47.34 while gold fell 0.70%, extending last week’s 6.18% decline (gold: 4.56%).
  • The Dollar and Treasury yields were little changed, so Monday’s extra silver weakness points to risk aversion, with Nikkei down 2.42% and KOSPI down 3.59%.
  • The gold/silver ratio rose 2.20% to 81.425, breaking above 80.110, with 84.481 the next target and 76.299 the support.
  • Silver faces support at 46.48, and a break lower would open 42.01, while 49.67 and 53.72 are the resistance levels for the bearish view.
  • US equities and Nvidia’s Tuesday earnings are the next tests of whether risk sentiment keeps driving silver lower.

Stay ahead of silver’s $46.48 support test and the risk signals that could decide the path toward $42—join the ActionForex Telegram channel for regular market updates and analysis.

headline: Eurozone Industrial Production Rises 0.2%, but Deeper Annual Decline Clouds Outlook
html_content:
Eurozone industrial production returned to modest growth in September, rising 0.2% mom after a 0.5% contraction in August, but fell short of market expectations for a 0.3% increase. The rebound ended three consecutive months of declining output, although annual production deteriorated further, with the contraction deepening from 1.1% to 1.5% yoy. Across the broader EU, industrial production rose 0.5% mom following a 0.3% decline in August, while annual output fell 0.8%. The divergence between the eurozone’s modest monthly improvement and worsening annual performance suggests that industrial activity is showing tentative signs of stabilization rather than a sustained recovery.

The sector breakdown revealed uneven performance. Intermediate goods production rebounded from a 0.7% decline to 0.7% growth mom, while durable consumer goods output improved from -0.1% to 1.3%. However, energy production fell 1.7%, reversing the previous month’s marginal 0.1% decline into a substantially sharper contraction, while capital goods output stagnated after rising 0.7% in August. Non-durable consumer goods production declined another 0.4%, following consecutive 2.8% monthly falls in July and August. On an annual basis, non-durable consumer goods remained the weakest category, contracting 7.5%, highlighting persistent weakness in an important segment of industrial activity.

Performance also varied significantly across major economies. Germany’s industrial production growth accelerated from 1.0% to 1.3% mom, while Italy rebounded from a 1.2% contraction to 1.2% growth and Spain recovered from -0.8% to 0.9%. France, however, recorded a second consecutive monthly decline of 0.5%, while Ireland’s output plunged 5.5% for a second straight month, leaving annual production down 19.1%. The contrasting national performances help explain why improving activity in several major economies translated into only a limited eurozone rebound. With industrial output still below its May level and annual production contracting more sharply, September’s figures provide insufficient evidence that the sector has established a durable recovery.

Key Takeaways

  • Modest rebound misses expectations: Eurozone industrial production rose 0.2% mom in September after three consecutive monthly declines, but missed the 0.3% forecast as annual output contracted further by 1.5%.
  • Industrial improvement remains uneven: Intermediate and durable consumer goods recovered, while energy production fell sharply, capital goods stagnated and non-durable consumer goods remained weak.
  • Divergent national performances cloud recovery: Germany, Italy and Spain recorded stronger production, but continued weakness in France and a sharp Irish contraction limited the broader improvement.

On an annual basis, non-durable consumer goods remained the weakest category, contracting 7.5%, highlighting persistent weakness in an important segment of industrial activity. Performance also varied significantly across major economies. Germany’s industrial production growth accelerated from 1.0% to 1.3% mom, while Italy rebounded from a 1.2% contraction to 1.2% growth and Spain recovered from -0.8% to 0.9%. France, however, recorded a second consecutive monthly decline of 0.5%, while Ireland’s output plunged 5.5% for a second straight month, leaving annual production down 19.1%. The contrasting national performances help explain why improving activity in several major economies translated into only a limited eurozone rebound. With industrial output still below its May level and annual production contracting more sharply, September’s figures provide insufficient evidence that the sector has established a durable recovery.
