headline: Canada CPI Holds at 3.1%, but Softer Core Inflation Challenges Further BoC Tightening
html_content:
Canada’s inflation rate is still above 3%, but the latest figures suggest that price pressures beneath the headline are considerably less threatening. Annual CPI held at 3.1% in October, undershooting expectations for 3.2%, while monthly inflation came in at 0.2% against a 0.3% forecast. More importantly, CPI-median stayed at 2.0% and CPI-trim slipped from a revised 1.9% to 1.8%, while inflation excluding energy eased from 2.1% to 2.0%. CPI-common edged up from 2.4% to 2.5%, preventing an entirely uniform picture of moderation. Nevertheless, with several underlying measures close to the BoC’s 2% target, the report raises questions about how urgently further interest rate increases are needed following October’s hike.

The main reason headline inflation remains elevated is the substantial contribution from energy. Gasoline prices surged 30.9% yoy, compared with 27.8% in September, although prices actually declined 2.5% during October itself. Statistics Canada attributed part of the annual acceleration to a base-year effect, as last year’s sharp gasoline price decline dropped out of the comparison. Inflation also picked up in some everyday spending categories. Grocery prices rose 2.0% yoy after increasing 1.7% in September, ending four months of slowing growth, while clothing inflation swung from -0.3% to 1.8%. Monthly clothing prices climbed 3.4%, the largest increase since September 2019, alongside higher shipping costs. The pressure was therefore not limited to energy, but neither did it produce a generalized acceleration in consumer prices.

Elsewhere, falling cellular service prices and slower rent inflation helped counter the increases. Cellular prices dropped 6.2% yoy, largely reflecting the disappearance of last October’s price increases from the annual calculation, while shelter inflation stood at 1.4% and rent inflation at 1.7%. These offsetting forces leave Canada’s inflation picture divided: energy and selected goods continue to push headline prices higher, while underlying inflation remains relatively restrained.

For the BoC, the distinction matters. Having raised rates to 2.50% in October, policymakers now face an inflation report that offers less immediate justification for another December increase than a stronger headline and core reading would have provided. Yet with CPI-common edging higher and some consumer categories showing renewed pressure, the data support a more cautious tightening assessment rather than a definitive end to further rate hikes.

headline: Yen Leads, Aussie Sinks as AI Selloff Spreads, but Bonds Offer Little Shelter
html_content:
Yen Gained Against All Seven Peers and Australian Dollar Weakened Across the Board as an AI-Led Equity Selloff Spread Through Global Markets, With Treasuries Offering Little Shelter

What’s happening: Yen gained against all seven major peers on Monday and Australian Dollar weakened across the board as an AI-led equity selloff spread, with South Korea’s KOSPI down 3.59% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 down 2.42%, while European equities were broadly stable and US Dow futures lost only 0.10%. Treasuries offered little shelter, with the two-year yield down just 1.4bps to 4.838% and the 10-year yield down 1.0bp to 5.129%.

Why it matters: Persistent Fed tightening expectations, with CME FedWatch at 93.7% for a 25bps December hike, limit the usual flight into government bonds, so elevated yields could amplify pressure on AI valuations and investment plans. The US cash open, Nvidia’s earnings on Tuesday and Wednesday’s Fed minutes are the next tests of whether the selling broadens.

Yen emerged as the strongest major currency on Monday, gaining against all seven peers, while Australian Dollar weakened across the board as an AI-led equity selloff spread through global markets. Dollar and Swiss Franc also occupied the stronger end of the currency spectrum, while Canadian and New Zealand Dollars lagged, reflecting a broader shift toward defensive positioning. The currency moves accompanied sharp declines in Asian technology shares, with South Korea’s KOSPI plunging 3.59% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 falling 2.42%. Yet the selling remained concentrated in technology-related assets, with European equities broadly stable and US Dow futures showing only modest losses. More concerning was the limited response from government bonds, as Treasury yields declined only marginally despite mounting equity-market pressure.

Follow the AI-led selloff, Yen strength and the Treasury response on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

Nvidia Turmoil Sends Shockwaves Through AI Stocks

The latest wave of selling followed Nvidia’s leadership upheaval, with Jensen Huang stepping down as CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress assuming the role on an interim basis. The disruption has heightened uncertainty surrounding the world’s leading AI chipmaker ahead of its earnings announcement on Tuesday. Nvidia shares were down around 2.7% in premarket trading, while its market capitalization had fallen to approximately $3.9 trillion by Friday from about $5.8 trillion in early October. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added to the uncertainty over the weekend, calling for a substantial management shakeup and greater scrutiny of compliance with export controls.

The pressure has spread particularly strongly through Asian semiconductor stocks. South Korea’s SK Hynix fell more than 5.6% during the session, while Samsung Electronics and Taiwan’s TSMC were also under pressure. In Japan, semiconductor equipment maker Advantest dropped almost 10%, Tokyo Electron lost 5.2% and SoftBank declined 4.2%, according to intraday reports. The broader selloff pushed KOSPI down 3.59% and Nikkei 225 lower by 2.42%, although Hong Kong’s Hang Seng managed a 0.49% gain.

European markets showed considerably greater resilience. Around midday, FTSE 100 was up 0.32%, CAC 40 gained 0.23% and DAX slipped just 0.10%, although semiconductor-related shares remained under pressure. US futures pointed to a similarly concentrated pattern, with Nasdaq-100 futures down 1.41%, compared with losses of 0.64% for S&P 500 futures and just 0.10% for Dow futures.

Equity Moves at a Glance

  • South Korea’s KOSPI: down 3.59%
  • Japan’s Nikkei 225: down 2.42%
  • SK Hynix: down more than 5.6%
  • Advantest: down almost 10% (intraday)
  • Tokyo Electron: down 5.2% (intraday)
  • SoftBank: down 4.2% (intraday)
  • Hong Kong’s Hang Seng: up 0.49%
  • FTSE 100: up 0.32% around midday
  • CAC 40: up 0.23% around midday
  • DAX: down 0.10% around midday
  • Nasdaq-100 futures: down 1.41%
  • S&P 500 futures: down 0.64%
  • Dow futures: down 0.10%

The defensive shift was also visible beyond equities. Yen strengthened against every other major currency in the ActionForex daily heat map, while Swiss Franc and Dollar were relatively firm. Australian Dollar was the weakest, with Canadian and New Zealand Dollars also lagging. Bitcoin fell 1.77%, Ether lost 1.99%, and silver declined 2.08%, substantially more than gold’s 0.36% drop.

The movements suggest that risk aversion is spreading across asset classes, although the scale of losses outside technology remains comparatively limited. Weakness in commodity currencies also reflects other pressures, including falling oil prices and disappointing Chinese economic data, rather than the AI selloff alone.

AI-Dependent Growth Faces Rising Borrowing Costs, but Treasuries Offer Little Relief

The broader significance of the technology selloff lies in the growing dependence of global economic activity on AI-related investment. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that the world economy has become increasingly reliant on AI as a source of growth, creating potential financial stability risks if investment confidence deteriorates.

According to media reports of her remarks, the IMF estimates circular financing arrangements among AI-related companies at slightly more than $1 trillion, with roughly two-thirds funded through debt. Although Georgieva described recent market movements as orderly, the rapid expansion of interconnected financing raises concerns about how a sustained correction in AI valuations could affect corporate investment and broader economic activity.

The vulnerability is heightened by rising borrowing costs. US Treasury yields surged last week as investors aggressively repriced Fed tightening expectations, with the two-year yield climbing 34bps and the 10-year yield rising 28bps. The Dollar also strengthened to a 2026 high. CME FedWatch pricing on Monday showed a 93.7% probability of a 25bps Fed hike in December, with the remaining 6.3% assigned to a larger 50bps increase.

Despite Monday’s equity losses, Treasuries provided little protection. The two-year yield edged down just 1.4bps to 4.838%, while the 10-year yield slipped only 1.0bp to 5.129%. The muted response suggests that persistent tightening expectations are limiting the scope for a conventional flight into government bonds.

Treasuries and Fed Pricing at a Glance

  • US two-year yield on Monday: down 1.4bps to 4.838%
  • US 10-year yield on Monday: down 1.0bp to 5.129%
  • Last week: two-year yield up 34bps and 10-year yield up 28bps
  • December Fed hike: 93.7% probability of 25bps, 6.3% of 50bps
  • Dollar: strengthened to a 2026 high last week

This creates an uncomfortable combination for risk assets. AI investment has become an important driver of corporate spending and global growth, much of it supported by borrowing, while the cost of financing that expansion is rising. If investor confidence weakens further, elevated yields could amplify the pressure on technology valuations and investment plans rather than cushion the adjustment.

Asian Economies Exposed as AI Growth Masks Domestic Weakness

The dependence on AI-related investment is particularly significant for Asian economies, where semiconductor production, technology exports and capital expenditure have become important sources of growth.

China’s latest October data highlighted the divergence between advanced manufacturing strength and weak domestic demand. Industrial production growth slowed from 5.5% to 4.8% yoy, retail sales growth weakened from 1.1% to just 0.4%, and fixed-asset investment contracted 8.1% over January–October. These figures contrasted with strong exports and continued expansion in high-tech manufacturing, illustrating the economy’s growing reliance on external demand and technology-oriented industries.

That dependence leaves China vulnerable if a prolonged correction in AI investment reduces demand for technology equipment and related products. However, the Hang Seng’s positive performance on Monday suggests that the equity selloff was not uniformly distributed across the region.

Japan faces a different but related challenge. Its economy contracted 0.1% annualized in Q3, missing expectations for 0.3% growth, as weak household consumption and net exports outweighed stronger business investment. The Nikkei initially fell around 0.6% following the GDP release before extending its decline to 2.42%, suggesting that technology-related selling added to the pressure from disappointing domestic growth.

China and Japan Data at a Glance

  • China industrial production: 4.8% yoy, down from 5.5%
  • China retail sales: 0.4% yoy, down from 1.1%
  • China fixed-asset investment: contracted 8.1% over January–October
  • Japan Q3 GDP: down 0.1% annualized, against expectations for 0.3% growth
  • Nikkei after the GDP release: initially down around 0.6%, extending to 2.42%

The contrasting performance of Asian markets reinforces the central vulnerability: AI-linked production and investment have helped offset weakness elsewhere in several economies. A prolonged technology downturn could therefore affect not only equity valuations but also some of the growth drivers supporting regional economic activity.

Concentrated Technology Weakness Meets High Financing Costs

The immediate test comes with Monday’s US cash market opening. If weakness spreads from Nasdaq into the S&P 500 and Dow, the argument that losses remain concentrated in technology would become less convincing. Conversely, stabilization in technology stocks, accompanied by fading Yen and Swiss Franc strength, would suggest that the broader risk-off adjustment is easing.

US Cash Open: Two Outcomes

Scenario Implication
Weakness spreads from Nasdaq into the S&P 500 and Dow The argument that losses remain concentrated in technology becomes less convincing
Technology stocks stabilize, with Yen and Swiss Franc strength fading Suggests the broader risk-off adjustment is easing

Attention will then turn to Nvidia’s earnings announcement on Tuesday after the US close. Investors will assess whether the company’s financial performance and outlook can restore confidence following its leadership disruption. The reaction will be particularly important for Asian semiconductor stocks when regional trading resumes on Wednesday.

Wednesday’s Fed minutes provide another potential catalyst. Markets will look for indications of how policymakers assess inflation risks and whether support is building for a more aggressive tightening pace. Any further hawkish repricing could keep Treasury yields elevated, limiting the protection normally offered by government bonds during equity-market declines.

Anthropic’s planned market debut on Thursday will provide an additional test of investor appetite for AI-related assets.

For now, the market picture is one of concentrated technology weakness accompanied by broader, but relatively modest, defensive positioning. Yen and Swiss Franc strength show that risk aversion is extending into currencies, while the limited Treasury rally highlights the constraints imposed by elevated interest rates. The critical question is whether Nvidia can stabilize confidence before the combination of weakening AI valuations and high financing costs begins to affect broader markets and economic growth.

Related Coverage

Fed and BoJ Policy

  • Fed’s Inflation Fight Shifts to Pace as Schmid Rejects Excuses, Collins Backs Gradual Hikes: The Fed’s inflation fight is increasingly focused on the pace of further tightening. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid rejected arguments that supply shocks and AI-driven demand are beyond monetary policy’s control, insisting the central bank has the tools and responsibility to restore price stability. Boston Fed President Susan Collins supported gradual rate increases, acknowledging stronger inflation and labor data while warning that higher market yields may already be restraining demand. Their comments reinforce the tightening outlook without endorsing the full rate path priced by markets.
  • BoJ’s Takata Urges Faster Rate Hikes as Weak Yen and Low Real Rates Threaten Inflation: BoJ board member Hajime Takata is calling for a fundamental shift in Japan’s monetary policy, urging faster and more flexible rate hikes now that underlying inflation has effectively reached 2%. He wants the policy rate moved closer to a neutral level, warning that exceptionally low real interest rates could weaken the Yen and intensify imported inflation. Takata sees resilient corporate earnings, stronger balance sheets and AI-related investment as supporting further tightening. However, Japan’s Q3 GDP contraction highlights the tension between rising inflation risks and fragile household demand, leaving the timing of another BoJ hike uncertain.

Silver and Currencies

  • Silver Sinks Toward $42 as Risk Aversion Adds to Dollar and Yield Pressure: Silver extended its selloff on Monday, falling nearly 3% to around $47.34 as weakness across Asian equities added to pressure from last week’s sharp rise in Treasury yields and the Dollar. Silver declined more than three times as much as gold, while the gold/silver ratio broke above 80.11 toward its next target at 84.48. With yields and the Dollar largely unchanged on Monday, the latest underperformance appears more closely associated with deteriorating risk sentiment. Technically, $46.48 is the immediate support, with a decisive break exposing $42.01 and potentially extending the larger downtrend.
  • Canada CPI Holds at 3.1%, but Softer Core Inflation Challenges Further BoC Tightening: Canada’s inflation held at 3.1% yoy in October, below expectations for an increase to 3.2%, while monthly CPI rose a softer-than-expected 0.2%. Underlying inflation was relatively contained, with CPI-median unchanged at 2.0% and CPI-trim easing to 1.8%, although CPI-common edged higher to 2.5%. Gasoline inflation accelerated to 30.9% yoy, while grocery and clothing prices also strengthened, but slower rent inflation and falling cellular service prices provided offsets. The divergence between elevated headline inflation and moderate underlying pressures challenges the urgency of another near-term BoC rate hike.
  • Canada CPI Today, UK CPI Wednesday: Can Inflation Finally Break GBP/CAD’s Range?: GBP/CAD faced a potentially decisive week, with Canada releasing October CPI on Monday and UK inflation following on Wednesday. Both the BoC and BoE have recently raised interest rates, but broadly parallel tightening expectations have kept the cross between 1.8604 and 1.9042. OIS markets price approximately 79bps of additional BoC tightening and 91bps for the BoE over roughly the next year. Canada’s inflation report had greater potential to reshape immediate rate expectations, while UK CPI will test the more extensive tightening already priced, and a meaningful divergence could finally challenge GBP/CAD’s consolidation.

Eurozone and Asia-Pacific Data

  • Eurozone Industrial Production Rises 0.2%, but Deeper Annual Decline Clouds Outlook: Eurozone industrial production returned to growth in September, rising 0.2% mom after a 0.5% decline in August, but missed expectations for a 0.3% increase. The modest rebound ended three consecutive monthly contractions, although annual output deteriorated further, falling 1.5% yoy. Intermediate goods and durable consumer goods recovered, while energy production declined sharply and capital goods stagnated. Germany and Italy posted stronger output, but France and Ireland continued to struggle, suggesting tentative stabilization rather than a sustained industrial recovery.
  • China Industrial Output Slows to 4.8%, Retail Sales Growth Falls to 0.4%: China’s October economic data revealed further weakness in domestic demand as industrial production, retail sales and fixed-asset investment all missed forecasts. Industrial output growth slowed from 5.5% to 4.8% yoy, while retail sales growth weakened from 1.1% to just 0.4%. Fixed-asset investment contracted 8.1% over January–October, with declines extending beyond property into manufacturing and infrastructure. High-tech manufacturing continued to outperform, expanding 17.6%, while strong exports provided external support, reinforcing concerns about China’s dependence on technology-driven production and overseas demand.
  • Japan GDP Contracts as Consumer Spending Falters, Business Investment Offers Rare Bright Spot: Japan’s economy contracted for the first time in four quarters, with real GDP falling 0.1% annualized in Q3 after growing 1.4% in Q2. Private consumption declined 0.3% for a second consecutive quarter, while net exports subtracted 0.6 percentage point from growth. Business investment provided a rare bright spot, rising 1.6% on demand for automation, digitalization and AI-related technologies. However, final sales of domestic product fell 2.1% annualized, exposing deeper weakness beneath the modest headline contraction.
  • NZ BNZ Services Hits Highest Since 2023 as Stronger Activity Outpaces Hiring: New Zealand’s services sector strengthened in October, with the BNZ–BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index rising from 50.9 to 51.7, its highest since 2023. Activity/Sales climbed from 50.4 to 52.6, while New Orders improved to 53.0, suggesting earlier demand gains are translating into stronger business activity. However, employment remained just below the expansion threshold at 49.9, and discretionary consumer services continued to struggle. The GDP-weighted composite index also rose to 52.2, pointing to broader economic improvement, although stronger activity has yet to generate meaningful hiring growth.

FAQ

Why did the Yen strengthen and the Australian Dollar weaken on Monday?

Yen gained against all seven peers and Australian Dollar weakened across the board as an AI-led equity selloff spread and investors shifted toward defensive positioning, with Swiss Franc and Dollar also firm. Weakness in commodity currencies, including Australian, Canadian and New Zealand Dollars, also reflects other pressures such as falling oil prices and disappointing Chinese economic data, so the AI selloff is not the only driver.

Why aren’t US Treasuries providing shelter from the AI selloff?

Persistent Fed tightening expectations are limiting the scope for a conventional flight into government bonds. The two-year yield edged down just 1.4bps to 4.838% and the 10-year slipped only 1.0bp to 5.129% on Monday, after rising 34bps and 28bps last week, while CME FedWatch showed a 93.7% probability of a 25bps December hike and 6.3% for 50bps. If investor confidence weakens further, elevated yields could amplify pressure on technology valuations and investment plans rather than cushion the adjustment.

Why is the AI selloff a concern beyond technology stocks?

The IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva warned that the world economy has become increasingly reliant on AI as a source of growth, with circular financing arrangements among AI-related companies estimated at slightly more than $1 trillion, roughly two-thirds funded through debt. Asian economies are particularly exposed: China’s October data showed strong high-tech output alongside weak retail sales and investment, and Japan’s economy contracted 0.1% annualized in Q3. A prolonged technology downturn could therefore affect growth drivers as well as equity valuations.

Key Takeaways

  1. Yen gained against all seven major peers on Monday while Australian Dollar weakened across the board, with Dollar and Swiss Franc also at the stronger end and Canadian and New Zealand Dollars lagging.
  2. Nvidia’s leadership upheaval, with Huang stepping down and Kress interim CEO, drove the latest selling, and its market capitalization fell to approximately $3.9 trillion by Friday from about $5.8 trillion in early October ahead of Tuesday’s earnings.
  3. Asian technology shares fell sharply, with KOSPI down 3.59% and Nikkei 225 down 2.42%, while FTSE 100 and CAC 40 were up and DAX slipped just 0.10%, and Dow futures lost only 0.10%.
  4. Weakness in commodity currencies also reflects falling oil prices and disappointing Chinese economic data, rather than the AI selloff alone.
  5. IMF Managing Director Georgieva warned the world economy is increasingly reliant on AI, with circular financing arrangements estimated at slightly more than $1 trillion, roughly two-thirds funded through debt.
  6. Treasuries provided little protection, with the two-year yield down 1.4bps to 4.838% and the 10-year down 1.0bp to 5.129% after last week’s 34bps and 28bps rises, while FedWatch showed 93.7% for a 25bps December hike and 6.3% for 50bps.
  7. China’s October data and Japan’s Q3 GDP contraction show Asian growth leaning on AI-linked production, and Nvidia’s Tuesday earnings and Wednesday’s Fed minutes are the next tests of whether selling broadens.

What to Watch Next

The first test is the US cash market opening: weakness spreading from Nasdaq into the S&P 500 and Dow would undermine the view that losses are concentrated in technology, while stabilization with fading Yen and Swiss Franc strength would suggest the risk-off adjustment is easing.

Nvidia’s earnings on Tuesday after the US close will show whether its financial performance and outlook can restore confidence, with Asian semiconductor stocks reacting when trading resumes on Wednesday. Wednesday’s Fed minutes could show whether support is building for a more aggressive tightening pace, and Anthropic’s planned market debut on Thursday will test investor appetite for AI-related assets.

Yet the selling remained concentrated in technology-related assets, with European equities broadly stable and US Dow futures showing only modest losses. More concerning was the limited response from government bonds, as Treasury yields declined only marginally despite mounting equity-market pressure. Follow the AI-led selloff, Yen strength and the Treasury response on the ActionForex Telegram channel. Nvidia Turmoil Sends Shockwaves Through AI Stocks The latest wave of selling followed Nvidia’s leadership upheaval, with Jensen Huang stepping down as CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress assuming the role on an interim basis. The disruption has heightened uncertainty surrounding the world’s leading AI chipmaker ahead of its earnings announcement on Tuesday. Nvidia shares were down around 2.7% in premarket trading, while its market capitalization had fallen to approximately $3.9 trillion by Friday from about $5.8 trillion in early October. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added to the uncertainty over the weekend, calling for a substantial management shakeup and greater scrutiny of compliance with export controls. The pressure has spread particularly strongly through Asian semiconductor stocks. South Korea’s SK Hynix fell more than 5.6% during the session, while Samsung Electronics and Taiwan’s TSMC were also under pressure. In Japan, semiconductor equipment maker Advantest dropped almost 10%, Tokyo Electron lost 5.2% and SoftBank declined 4.2%, according to intraday reports. The broader selloff pushed KOSPI down 3.59% and Nikkei 225 lower by 2.42%, although Hong Kong’s Hang Seng managed a 0.49% gain. European markets showed considerably greater resilience. Around midday, FTSE 100 was up 0.32%, CAC 40 gained 0.23% and DAX slipped just 0.10%, although semiconductor-related shares remained under pressure. US futures pointed to a similarly concentrated pattern, with Nasdaq-100 futures down 1.41%, compared with losses of 0.64% for S&P 500 futures and just 0.10% for Dow futures. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that the world economy has become increasingly reliant on AI as a source of growth, creating potential financial stability risks if investment confidence deteriorates. According to media reports of her remarks, the IMF estimates circular financing arrangements among AI-related companies at slightly more than $1 trillion, with roughly two-thirds funded through debt. Although Georgieva described recent market movements as orderly, the rapid expansion of interconnected financing raises concerns about how a sustained correction in AI valuations could affect corporate investment and broader economic activity. The vulnerability is heightened by rising borrowing costs. US Treasury yields surged last week as investors aggressively repriced Fed tightening expectations, with the two-year yield climbing 34bps and the 10-year yield rising 28bps. The Dollar also strengthened to a 2026 high. CME FedWatch pricing on Monday showed a 93.7% probability of a 25bps Fed hike in December, with the remaining 6.3% assigned to a larger 50bps increase. Despite Monday’s equity losses, Treasuries provided little protection. The two-year yield edged down just 1.4bps to 4.838%, while the 10-year yield slipped only 1.0bp to 5.129%. The muted response suggests that persistent tightening expectations are limiting the scope for a conventional flight into government bonds. AI investment has become an important driver of corporate spending and global growth, much of it supported by borrowing, while the cost of financing that expansion is rising. If investor confidence weakens further, elevated yields could amplify the pressure on technology valuations and investment plans rather than cushion the adjustment. Asian Economies Exposed as AI Growth Masks Domestic Weakness The dependence on AI-related investment is particularly significant for Asian economies, where semiconductor production, technology exports and capital expenditure have become important sources of growth. China’s latest October data highlighted the divergence between advanced manufacturing strength and weak domestic demand. Industrial production growth slowed from 5.5% to 4.8% yoy, retail sales growth weakened from 1.1% to just 0.4%, and fixed-asset investment contracted 8.1% over January–October. These figures contrasted with strong exports and continued expansion in high-tech manufacturing, illustrating the economy’s growing reliance on external demand and technology-oriented industries. That dependence leaves China vulnerable if a prolonged correction in AI investment reduces demand for technology equipment and related products. headline: Fed’s Hammack Sees Continued Tightening Need, Warsh Highlights AI Uncertainty
html_content:
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack reiterated her preference for gradual interest rate increases, arguing that smaller, predictable adjustments allow businesses and households to plan more effectively. “I like moving in smaller increments,” she said in a Bloomberg TV interview, but stressed that larger hikes remain an option if inflation worsens. “If we get behind the curve and we need to put more restriction in, we absolutely can move in those larger increments.” Hammack noted that inflation pressures have been broadening rather than easing, while the labour market remains relatively stable but is showing emerging signs of hiring tightness. She warned that both inflation and employment conditions could eventually point toward greater monetary restraint, potentially requiring a higher terminal policy rate.

Hammack also argued that financial conditions are not yet sufficiently restrictive to slow economic growth. Addressing concerns that heavy borrowing by AI-related companies has contributed to rising Treasury yields, she said corporate AI issuance remains relatively small compared with government borrowing. “While the scale of AI-related issuance is large for corporates, it’s very small relative to governments,” she said, rejecting suggestions that AI financing is the main explanation for higher yields. Instead, she attributed higher government borrowing costs primarily to strong economic growth and expectations of further Fed rate increases. Her assessment reinforces the case for continued tightening while pointing to Fed policy expectations, rather than AI financing demand, as a more important driver of elevated Treasury yields.

Separately, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh highlighted both the economic opportunities and risks associated with artificial intelligence during a conference in San Francisco. He suggested that emerging technology could “supercharge idea generation,” potentially supporting sustained productivity gains and stronger economic growth. However, Warsh warned that AI could also disrupt employment and impose substantial economic costs if anticipated investment returns disappoint. Emphasizing the uncertainty surrounding AI’s economic impact, he said, “Our job is to prepare for whatever comes next.” Warsh noted that technological adoption would have important monetary policy implications over time but offered no specific guidance on near-term interest rate decisions.

Key Takeaways

  • Hammack favors gradual tightening: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack supports smaller, predictable rate hikes but remains open to larger increases if inflation pressures continue to worsen.
  • Inflation and labour market risks point to further restraint: Broadening inflation, emerging hiring tightness and financial conditions that are not sufficiently restrictive could require a higher eventual policy rate.
  • Warsh highlights AI uncertainty: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh sees potential for stronger productivity and economic growth from AI, but warns of employment disruption and disappointing investment returns, without offering near-term monetary policy guidance.

headline: RBNZ Sees Rising Global Financial Risks, but New Zealand Banks Remain Resilient
html_content:
RBNZ warned in its November Financial Stability Report that global financial stability risks have continued to increase, raising the possibility of a significant shock to New Zealand’s economy and financial system. Heightened geopolitical tensions, elevated government bond yields and stretched equity valuations, particularly among AI-related companies, have left financial markets vulnerable to a correction. Nevertheless, Governor Anna Breman emphasized that domestic financial institutions remain well positioned to withstand turbulence. “While the global economic environment is uncertain, our financial institutions remain well placed to withstand financial market turbulence and support the economy,” she said.

The central bank highlighted how global vulnerabilities could reinforce one another. Conflict in the Middle East continues to threaten energy supplies and trade, while higher government bond yields are adding pressure on heavily indebted economies. At the same time, elevated AI-related equity valuations and growing financial links between technology companies could amplify a market correction. Although AI investment has supported global growth and Asian exports, a sharp reversal could weaken external demand, increase risk aversion and tighten financial conditions. For New Zealand, these shocks could translate into weaker export demand, higher import costs and more expensive or less accessible offshore funding.

Despite these external risks, RBNZ assessed the domestic banking system as fundamentally sound. Banks maintain strong capital and liquidity positions despite some narrowing of lending margins, while recent stress tests indicate that banks and insurers could withstand severe financial shocks. Mortgage lending growth remains modest, limiting the build-up of housing-related vulnerabilities, although property markets remain subdued, particularly in Auckland and Wellington. Domestic financial stress has also eased from last year’s peak, but the improvement remains uneven. “Smaller businesses and sectors reliant on discretionary household spending continue to face challenges,” Breman noted.

The report also identified growing operational risks from artificial intelligence, particularly increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks and dependence on common technology providers. RBNZ urged financial institutions to strengthen cybersecurity, maintain critical services and improve their ability to recover from disruptions. Overall, the report presents a contrast between rising external vulnerabilities and a domestic financial system with substantial capacity to absorb shocks. While New Zealand cannot avoid the economic consequences of a major global downturn, strong banking buffers and subdued credit growth reduce the risk that external turbulence develops into a domestic financial crisis.

Key Takeaways

  • Global financial risks are rising: RBNZ warns that geopolitical tensions, elevated government bond yields and stretched AI-related equity valuations could interact and amplify financial market shocks.
  • New Zealand faces external economic and funding pressures: A global downturn could weaken export demand, increase import costs and make offshore funding more expensive or less accessible.
  • Domestic financial system remains resilient: Strong bank capital and liquidity buffers, successful stress tests and modest mortgage lending growth provide protection, although smaller businesses and discretionary spending sectors remain under pressure.

Full RBNZ release here.

headline: RBA’s Bullock Flags Triple Inflation Threat from AI Spending, Oil and Expectations
html_content:
RBA Governor Michele Bullock warned that Australia’s inflation outlook faces three significant upside risks: surging investment in AI and data centres, persistently elevated oil prices, and the possibility of inflation expectations becoming entrenched above the central bank’s 2–3% target. Speaking at the ASIC Forum in Sydney, Bullock highlighted the inflationary impact of accelerated AI-related spending at a time when the economy has limited spare capacity. “There is a lot of expenditure going on here and this is adding to demand and pressure on resources at a time that we don’t really have space to absorb it,” she said. While AI investment could support longer-term productivity, the immediate surge in demand risks adding to price pressures before those benefits materialize.

Bullock also warned that oil prices could remain elevated for longer than assumed in the RBA’s inflation forecasts, delaying the expected easing in headline inflation. More concerning for the medium-term outlook is the possibility that businesses and households begin accepting persistently higher inflation as normal. She pointed to early indications from the RBA’s business liaison program that some firms are considering whether “3, 3.5% is the new normal for inflation.” If such expectations become embedded in pricing and wage-setting decisions, bringing inflation back within the 2–3% target could become substantially more difficult. However, Bullock’s remarks indicated an emerging risk rather than evidence that inflation expectations have already become entrenched.

The combination of strong investment demand, persistent energy costs and potentially rising inflation expectations reinforces the RBA’s concern that inflation could prove more difficult to contain than currently projected. Nevertheless, Bullock acknowledged downside risks from falling home prices and broader economic uncertainty, including geopolitical conflicts and the unpredictable effects of AI. Her comments underscore the need to maintain sufficient monetary restraint until inflation pressures ease sustainably, although she provided no explicit guidance on the timing or likelihood of further interest rate increases.

Key Takeaways

  • AI investment adds to inflation pressures: RBA Governor Michele Bullock warned that surging AI and data centre spending is increasing demand for resources when Australia’s economy has limited spare capacity.
  • Oil prices threaten to delay disinflation: Persistently elevated energy costs could prevent headline inflation from easing as anticipated in the RBA’s forecasts.
  • Inflation expectations pose a longer-term risk: Early signs that businesses may regard 3–3.5% inflation as normal raise concerns about price pressures becoming entrenched above the RBA’s 2–3% target.

headline: RBA Minutes Reveal Hawkish Majority, but Three Dissenters Warn of Sharper Downturn
html_content:
Minutes of RBA’s November 2–3 meeting revealed a clear division over the risks of further monetary tightening, with six members voting to raise the cash rate by 25bps to 4.85%, while three preferred to hold at 4.60%. The majority judged that inflation pressures had strengthened and that the existing level of interest rates was “not clearly sufficient” to bring inflation sustainably back to target. In particular, members considered the risks of leaving monetary policy insufficiently restrictive greater than those of tightening too aggressively, citing persistent inflation, stronger-than-expected domestic capacity pressures and signs of continued economic resilience.

The inflation outlook had deteriorated significantly since August, with both headline and underlying inflation now expected to remain above 3% until late 2027, before returning to the midpoint of the 2–3% target around mid-2028. Stronger market services inflation, persistent unit labour cost pressures and a reassessment of the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation suggested that domestic spare capacity was more limited than previously estimated. Members also considered the possibility that Australia’s neutral interest rate had risen, meaning the existing cash rate might be providing less restraint than assumed. These developments strengthened the majority’s view that another increase was warranted, even after 100bps of tightening earlier in the year.

External and investment-related pressures added to the inflation risks. Oil prices had risen 20–25% since August, while the RBA’s forecasts assumed a substantial decline over the following two years, leaving inflation vulnerable if energy costs stayed elevated. Meanwhile, strong AI-related investment was supporting economic activity but also contributing to capacity constraints and higher prices for some technology goods. Data centre developers accounted for at least one-fifth of the increase in Australian business debt this year, although investors had become more cautious about heavily indebted AI-related companies. The combination highlighted AI investment’s dual role as a source of near-term demand and a potential vulnerability if financing conditions deteriorate.

The three dissenting members placed greater weight on the danger of excessive tightening, arguing that the full effects of this year’s 100bps of rate increases had yet to emerge. They pointed to a larger-than-expected rise in unemployment, the substantial housing market downturn and the possibility that weakening demand could already be sufficient to bring inflation under control. The minutes recorded their concern that the economy might be approaching a “materially sharper downturn.” While the majority favored stronger action against persistent inflation, the split decision underscored uncertainty over how much additional restraint the economy could absorb. The Board offered no commitment to further hikes, leaving upcoming inflation, employment and activity data central to the policy outlook.

Key Takeaways

  • Hawkish majority backs further restraint: RBA minutes revealed a 6–3 vote to raise the cash rate to 4.85%, with the majority judging that existing monetary restraint was not clearly sufficient to contain persistent inflation.
  • Inflation outlook deteriorates: Headline and underlying inflation are expected to remain above 3% until late 2027, with stronger domestic capacity pressures, elevated oil prices and AI-related investment adding to inflation risks.
  • Three dissenters warn of sharper downturn: The minority preferred to assess the effects of 100bps of tightening already delivered, citing rising unemployment, housing weakness and the possibility of a materially sharper economic slowdown.

Full RBA minutes here.

headline: RBNZ Survey Shows Near-Term Inflation Fears Rising, but Long-Term Expectations Ease
html_content:
New Zealand’s one-year-ahead inflation expectations rose sharply from 2.60% to 2.92% in RBNZ’s November Survey of Expectations, approaching the upper boundary of the central bank’s 1–3% inflation target range. However, longer-term expectations remained relatively well anchored, suggesting that respondents anticipate more persistent near-term inflation without expecting price pressures to become permanently entrenched. Two-year-ahead expectations edged up from 2.34% to 2.36%, while five-year expectations declined from 2.31% to 2.17% and ten-year expectations eased from 2.20% to 2.13%. The divergence emerged despite annual CPI inflation slowing from 4.1% to 3.7% in Q3, indicating that respondents have become less confident about the pace of disinflation over the coming year.

Interest rate expectations also shifted higher. The mean expectation for the Official Cash Rate at the end of 2026 increased to 3.05%, compared with the current OCR of 2.75%, while the one-year-ahead expectation rose from 3.21% to 3.40%. The combination of higher near-term inflation and OCR expectations points to growing anticipation of additional monetary tightening, even as longer-term inflation expectations remain close to 2%. However, the figures represent survey forecasts from business leaders and professional forecasters rather than market-implied probabilities or RBNZ policy guidance. The central bank’s next Monetary Policy Statement is scheduled for December 9.

The broader economic outlook was mixed. One-year-ahead GDP growth expectations increased from 2.16% to 2.34%, while two-year expectations rose from 2.43% to 2.59%. Expected unemployment was unchanged at 5.24% over one year and eased from 4.90% to 4.85% over two years, while wage inflation expectations rose to 2.90% over one year but declined to 2.85% over two years. Meanwhile, housing expectations weakened substantially, with anticipated house price growth falling from 1.47% to 0.51% over one year and from 3.27% to 2.43% over two years. The survey therefore presents an economy expected to regain growth momentum while inflation concerns persist and the housing market remains subdued. The responses were collected between October 23 and 30, before the latest labour market release showed unemployment rising to 5.7%.

Inflation and Interest Rate Expectations

Indicator Current Previous Change
CPI inflation — 1 year 2.92% 2.60% +32bps
CPI inflation — 2 years 2.36% 2.34% +2bps
CPI inflation — 5 years 2.17% 2.31% -14bps
CPI inflation — 10 years 2.13% 2.20% -7bps
OCR — End-2026 3.05% 2.73% +32bps
OCR — 1 year 3.40% 3.21% +19bps

Economic and Housing Expectations

Indicator Current Previous Change
GDP growth — 1 year 2.34% 2.16% +18bps
GDP growth — 2 years 2.59% 2.43% +16bps
Unemployment — 1 year 5.24% 5.24% 0bps
Unemployment — 2 years 4.85% 4.90% -5bps
Wage inflation — 1 year 2.90% 2.78% +12bps
Wage inflation — 2 years 2.85% 2.93% -8bps
House price inflation — 1 year 0.51% 1.47% -96bps
House price inflation — 2 years 2.43% 3.27% -84bps

Note: Expectations are survey means from 44 business leaders and professional forecasters, collected October 23–30, 2026. OCR figures represent respondents’ forecasts, not market-implied probabilities.

Key Takeaways

  • Near-term inflation expectations jump: One-year expectations rose from 2.60% to 2.92%, while two-year expectations barely changed at 2.36%. Five- and ten-year expectations declined, indicating that longer-term inflation expectations remain relatively well anchored.
  • Respondents anticipate further RBNZ tightening: The expected OCR at end-2026 increased to 3.05%, while the one-year outlook rose to 3.40%, compared with the current rate of 2.75%.
  • Growth outlook improves, but housing weakens: One-year GDP growth expectations increased to 2.34%, while expected house price growth fell sharply to 0.51%, reflecting continued weakness in housing confidence.

Full RBNZ Survey of Expectations here.

headline: AUD/JPY Targets 105.22 as Risk Aversion Favors Yen, RBA–BoJ Rate Gap Set to Narrow
html_content:
TL;DR: Global risk aversion is the dominant driver pushing AUD/JPY lower, with the Yen in demand and the Aussie under pressure, and 105.22 is the next downside target. The expected narrowing of the RBA–BoJ rate gap is already priced, so risk appetite, starting with Nvidia’s earnings, is likely to set the near-term direction.

Why Is AUD/JPY Falling Despite Australia’s Rate Advantage?

AUD/JPY extended its decline on Tuesday, trading around 107.33 after breaking below key Fibonacci projection level at 107.63. Risk aversion remains the dominant near-term driver, with Yen benefiting from defensive demand while Australian Dollar struggles against a backdrop of falling global equities and growing concerns over AI-related investments. The weekly currency heat map showed Yen outperforming all seven major peers, while Aussie ranked second weakest, with AUD/JPY trading below last week’s low. Beyond the immediate market turbulence, OIS-implied expectations point to a narrowing RBA–BoJ interest rate differential through 2027, although much of that prospective convergence is already reflected in market pricing.

Global Risk Aversion Keeps AUD/JPY Under Pressure

The latest decline in AUD/JPY follows a broadening global equity selloff, initially centered on AI-related technology companies but increasingly affecting other sectors. US stocks suffered substantial losses on Monday, with Nasdaq Composite plunging 2.49%, S&P 500 falling 1.92%, and Dow Jones Industrial Average declining 1.41%. VIX surged 18.7% to 22.90, reflecting a sharp increase in market volatility.

  • Nasdaq Composite: −2.49%; S&P 500: −1.92%; Dow Jones: −1.41%
  • VIX: +18.7% to 22.90

Technology shares remained at the center of the selling. Nvidia dropped 4.12% ahead of its closely watched earnings announcement on Tuesday, as investors continued to assess the implications of the company’s leadership upheaval and the outlook for AI investment. However, weakness spread beyond the technology sector, with consumer staples the only S&P 500 sector recording gains during the afternoon session.

Selling pressure continued into Asian markets on Tuesday. Around 04:30 UTC, Nikkei 225 was down 1.28%, KOSPI had lost 1.91%, and Hang Seng was trading 0.77% lower. The declines followed Monday’s particularly sharp losses in Asian semiconductor stocks, including Japan’s Advantest, Tokyo Electron, and SoftBank.

The currency market response reinforced the defensive shift. Monday’s daily heat map showed Yen strengthening against all seven major currencies, while Australian Dollar weakened across the board. The weekly heat map continued to place Yen at the top, with Aussie near the bottom. AUD/JPY has consequently become a clear expression of the prevailing risk-off environment, combining the vulnerability of a growth-sensitive currency with the defensive appeal of Yen.

Notably, Yen strength persisted despite Japan’s disappointing Q3 GDP figures, which showed an annualized contraction of 0.1% against expectations for 0.3% growth. That divergence suggests global risk sentiment has been more influential than Japan’s near-term economic performance in driving the currency.

Australian Dollar also faces additional pressure from China, where October industrial production, retail sales, and investment all disappointed expectations. These developments provide a separate explanation for Aussie’s underperformance, although the immediate weakness in AUD/JPY remains closely aligned with deteriorating equity sentiment.

Tuesday’s currency movements have been less uniformly defensive than Monday’s, with Aussie recovering some ground against other commodity currencies. Nevertheless, AUD/JPY has continued to weaken, indicating that the relative strength of Yen remains important for the cross.

Follow AUD/JPY’s slide toward 105.22 and the risk-sentiment signals behind it on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

RBA–BoJ Rate Gap Expected to Narrow Through 2027

Beyond the immediate risk-off pressure, the medium-term interest rate outlook offers diminishing support for AUD/JPY.

The RBA’s cash rate currently stands at 4.85%, compared with BoJ’s policy rate of 1.25%, leaving a substantial 360bps interest rate advantage for Australian Dollar. However, OIS-implied pricing suggests that the differential is more likely to narrow than widen over the coming year.

Current pricing assigns just a 4.0% probability to another RBA rate hike in December, while implying a modest 6.2bps decline in the Australian policy rate over the next 12 months. By contrast, the probability of a BoJ hike in December stands at 83.6%, with approximately 66.1bps of tightening implied over the same period.

Taken together, these expectations point to a narrowing of the RBA–BoJ policy-rate gap by around 72bps over 12 months. By the end of 2027, the differential is projected to shrink by approximately 80bps to 280bps, with the Australian cash rate implied at 4.76% and the Japanese rate at 1.96%.

  • RBA cash rate 4.85% vs BoJ policy rate 1.25%: 360bps gap
  • December: 4.0% probability of an RBA hike; 83.6% probability of a BoJ hike
  • Next 12 months: RBA about −6.2bps; BoJ about +66.1bps (gap narrows by around 72bps)
  • End of 2027: gap about 280bps (RBA at 4.76%, BoJ at 1.96%)

The important qualification is that this convergence is already reflected in OIS pricing. It therefore represents a medium-term fundamental backdrop rather than a new catalyst for AUD/JPY selling. Further downward pressure from policy divergence would require expectations to shift more decisively toward BoJ tightening or away from RBA tightening.

The RBA’s November meeting minutes reinforced the uncertainty surrounding Australia’s policy outlook. The Board voted 6–3 to raise the cash rate to 4.85%, with the majority judging that inflation risks warranted additional restraint. However, three dissenting members preferred to wait for the effects of previous tightening, warning that the economy could be approaching a “materially sharper downturn.”

The minutes also highlighted competing pressures from persistent inflation, elevated oil prices, and strong AI-related investment on one side, and weakening housing conditions and rising unemployment on the other. With unemployment at 4.7% and the housing market experiencing a substantial downturn, the scope for further Australian tightening may be increasingly constrained by economic weakness.

Importantly, OIS-implied RBA expectations showed little reaction to the minutes, with December hike pricing remaining at 4.0%. The release therefore provided limited evidence of a fresh shift in monetary policy expectations.

For BoJ, the principal uncertainty is whether Japan’s economy can sustain the degree of tightening currently priced. The disappointing Q3 GDP reading and pressure from elevated energy import costs could eventually weigh on policy normalization. A reduction in expected BoJ tightening would help preserve Australia’s rate advantage, potentially limiting medium-term downside pressure on AUD/JPY.

ActionForex’s Technical View: AUD/JPY, 105.22 Next as Correction Deepens

AUD/JPY’s fall from 114.95 continued this week and broke through 61.8% projection of 114.95 to 108.62 from 111.55 at 107.63. There is no sign of bottoming yet, despite oversold condition in 4H RSI. Current decline should continue to 100% projection at 105.22 next.

On the upside, above 108.62 support turned resistance will bring consolidations first. But near term outlook will stay bearish as long as 111.55 resistance holds, in case of recovery.

In the bigger picture, decline from 114.95 is seen as correcting the uptrend from 86.03 (2025 low). The break below 55 W EMA supports this. The correction could extend to 38.2% retracement 86.03 to 114.95 at 103.90 before completion.

Nvidia Earnings and Economic Data to Test the Downtrend

Near-term attention will center on Nvidia’s earnings announcement after Tuesday’s US market close. A reassuring report could help stabilize technology shares and reduce defensive demand for Yen, potentially allowing AUD/JPY to consolidate after its recent decline. A disappointment would risk extending the equity selloff and reinforcing pressure on the cross.

Australia’s Q3 Wage Price Index, due Wednesday, will provide further evidence on domestic inflation pressures, with quarterly wage growth expected at 0.9%. Japan’s October trade figures will follow, offering another indication of how external demand and elevated import costs are affecting the economy.

Further ahead, the RBA’s December 8 decision and BoJ’s December 18 meeting will test the policy-rate paths currently implied by markets.

For now, the near-term direction of AUD/JPY remains closely tied to global risk appetite, while the expected narrowing in the RBA–BoJ rate differential reduces the prospect of additional support from Australia’s interest rate advantage. With the technical breakdown already in place, 105.22 remains the immediate downside objective, while 103.90 represents a possible deeper correction target if selling persists.

Key Takeaways

  • AUD/JPY traded around 107.33 after breaking the 107.63 projection level, with risk aversion the dominant driver as Yen outperformed all seven majors.
  • US stocks fell sharply on Monday (Nasdaq −2.49%, VIX +18.7% to 22.90), and Asian markets extended the weakness on Tuesday, ahead of Nvidia’s earnings after the US close.
  • Australia’s 360bps rate advantage over Japan is expected to narrow by around 72bps over 12 months, but that convergence is already priced and is a backdrop rather than a fresh catalyst.
  • The decline should continue to the 105.22 projection, with 103.90 a deeper correction target, while 108.62 and 111.55 are the resistance levels for the bearish view.
  • Australia’s Q3 Wage Price Index (Wednesday), Japan’s October trade figures, the RBA on December 8 and the BoJ on December 18 are the next tests.

Stay ahead of AUD/JPY’s slide toward 105.22 and the risk signals that could decide it—join the ActionForex Telegram channel for regular market updates and analysis.

headline: UK Unemployment Falls to 4.6%, but Payroll Losses and Weaker Hiring Tell Different Story
html_content:
UK unemployment rate fell from 4.7% to 4.6% in the three months to September, beating expectations for an unchanged reading, while the employment rate edged up from 75.3% to 75.4%. However, the improvement in headline unemployment was partly driven by changes in the Labour Force Survey sample rather than stronger underlying labour demand. ONS explained that respondents leaving the survey had unusually low employment and high unemployment compared with incoming participants, contributing to the latest improvement. On a non-overlapping quarterly basis, employment increased by 155,000 to 34.625 million, while unemployment fell by 88,000 to 1.684 million. Meanwhile, October’s Claimant Count increased by 33,200, exceeding expectations of 28,100.

More timely payroll and vacancy data painted a weaker picture. Payrolled employment fell by 34,000 in October to approximately 30.2 million, down 95,000 or 0.3% from a year earlier. September’s increase was revised from 13,000 to 20,000, while October’s preliminary estimate remains subject to revision. Meanwhile, job vacancies declined by 22,000, or 3.0%, to 690,000 in the three months to October, their lowest non-pandemic level since 2014. Vacancies fell across 11 of 18 industries, with reductions in administrative and support services, construction, and transport and storage. Smaller businesses accounted for the entire net quarterly decline, as vacancies among firms employing one to nine workers dropped by 22,000 to 73,000. ONS reported that higher labour and operating costs were discouraging recruitment, reinforcing evidence of weakening underlying hiring demand.

Wage pressures also moderated. Annual growth in regular earnings excluding bonuses slowed from 3.7% to 3.5% in the three months to September, below expectations of 3.6%, while total earnings growth eased from 3.8% to 3.6%. The slowdown in regular pay was driven largely by public-sector earnings as the effects of earlier pay-award timing continued to fade. Public-sector regular earnings rose 5.4% yoy, compared with 3.1% in the private sector, while real regular earnings increased just 0.2% using CPIH inflation. Taken together, declining payroll employment, falling vacancies and slower wage growth suggest labour demand and pay pressures are easing, despite the better unemployment headline. The divergence warrants caution in interpreting the latest improvement in unemployment, particularly given the survey-related distortion identified by ONS.

Key Takeaways

  • Unemployment falls, but improvement is partly statistical: The jobless rate declined from 4.7% to 4.6%, beating expectations, although changes in the Labour Force Survey sample contributed to the improvement.
  • Hiring demand continues to weaken: October payroll employment fell by 34,000, while vacancies declined to 690,000, their lowest non-pandemic level since 2014. Smaller businesses accounted for the entire net quarterly vacancy reduction.
  • Wage pressures moderate: Regular earnings growth slowed from 3.7% to 3.5%, below expectations, while total pay growth eased from 3.8% to 3.6%. The slowdown reinforces evidence of cooling labour demand, although public-sector pay-award timing contributed.

headline: NZD/USD Nears 2020 Low Despite Rising RBNZ Rate Hike Expectations
html_content:
TL;DR: NZD/USD is sliding toward its 2020 low even as RBNZ rate hike expectations rebuild, which points to global risk aversion rather than New Zealand policy as the driver. A decisive break of the 0.5467 2020 low would confirm the long-term downtrend is resuming.

Why Is NZD/USD Falling Even as RBNZ Hike Expectations Rise?

NZD/USD extended its decline this week to 0.54832, its lowest level since 2020, approaching the critical support area surrounding the 2020 low of 0.5467. The weakness comes despite a recovery in RBNZ rate hike expectations over the past week, with markets pricing substantial additional tightening through 2027. The divergence suggests New Zealand’s monetary policy outlook is not the principal explanation for Kiwi’s decline. Instead, broader risk aversion and defensive currency demand appear to be exerting greater influence, leaving NZD/USD vulnerable to a long-term technical breakdown even as domestic interest rate expectations become more supportive.

RBNZ Rate Hike Expectations Rebuild After October Hold

The RBNZ held its Official Cash Rate at 2.75% on October 28 in a narrow 4–3 decision, with three policymakers preferring an immediate increase to 3.00%. The hold surprised markets that had almost fully priced a hike beforehand, although Governor Anna Breman subsequently indicated that further increases were likely, potentially taking policy into restrictive territory.

OIS-implied pricing has since recovered. As of Tuesday morning, the December 9 meeting implied a policy rate around 2.96%, while subsequent meetings pointed to 3.11% in February, 3.24% in March and 3.45% by June 2027. The implied rate rises further to 3.64% in October 2027 and approximately 3.69% by year-end.

  • December 9: about 2.96%
  • February: 3.11%; March: 3.24%
  • June 2027: 3.45%; October 2027: 3.64%; year-end 2027: about 3.69%

The curve has shifted higher over the past week, but remains below levels prevailing before October’s surprise hold. December tightening is largely anticipated, although the precise probability of a 25bps hike depends on the relationship between OIS pricing and its underlying reference rate. Westpac Senior Economist Satish Ranchhod also expects an increase in December, citing firm underlying inflation pressures and the prospect of higher fuel costs lifting headline inflation.

The direction of recent repricing is important for NZD/USD. The market has added expected RBNZ tightening rather than reduced it, making domestic rate expectations an unlikely primary driver of the latest currency weakness.

Follow NZD/USD’s test of the 2020 low and the RBNZ outlook on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

RBNZ Survey Reinforces Near-Term Inflation Concerns

The RBNZ’s November Survey of Expectations offered little evidence of a fresh dovish shift. One-year inflation expectations rose from 2.60% to 2.92%, while two-year expectations edged up from 2.34% to 2.36%. However, longer-term measures moved in the opposite direction, with five-year expectations falling from 2.31% to 2.17% and ten-year expectations easing from 2.20% to 2.13%.

The combination indicates greater concern over near-term inflation without a corresponding deterioration in longer-term expectations. Survey respondents also raised their one-year OCR expectation from 3.21% to 3.40%, while the expected rate for the end of December stood at 3.05%, compared with 2.75% currently.

  • One-year inflation expectations: 2.60% to 2.92%; two-year: 2.34% to 2.36%
  • Five-year: 2.31% to 2.17%; ten-year: 2.20% to 2.13%
  • One-year OCR expectation: 3.21% to 3.40%; end-December expectation: 3.05% (OCR currently 2.75%)

The survey was conducted between October 23 and 30, spanning the RBNZ’s October decision and preceding this week’s market repricing. Its findings therefore provide context for the tightening outlook rather than evidence of a reaction to the latest currency decline. The one-year OCR expectation also implies somewhat less tightening than current OIS pricing, although the survey and market horizons are not identical.

Separately, the RBNZ’s Financial Stability Report described New Zealand’s financial system as resilient, while warning of risks from geopolitical tensions, higher government bond yields and stretched valuations, particularly among AI-related companies. Domestic housing conditions remained subdued, and financial pressures continued to affect smaller businesses and discretionary-spending sectors.

The report underscores New Zealand’s exposure to external financial shocks, but contains no direct monetary policy signal capable of explaining the latest NZD/USD decline.

Global Risk Aversion Outweighs Relative Rate Support

The broader currency and equity market picture offers a more plausible explanation for Kiwi’s weakness. The weekly currency heat map showed Yen, Dollar and Swiss Franc outperforming, while Australian and New Zealand Dollars ranked at the bottom. NZD/USD traded below the previous week’s low, consistent with the pressure facing growth-sensitive currencies.

Monday’s sharp US equity selloff reinforced the defensive environment. Nasdaq Composite plunged 2.49%, S&P 500 dropped 1.92%, and Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1.41%, while VIX reached 22.90. Concerns surrounding AI-related investment and technology valuations also weighed on Asian semiconductor shares. Disappointing Chinese retail sales, industrial production and investment figures added another headwind for currencies exposed to regional growth.

Relative interest rate expectations do not offer a compelling alternative explanation. CME FedWatch pricing indicated approximately 26bps of expected Fed tightening in December, slightly less than the roughly 27bps implied a week earlier. Over the same period, RBNZ tightening expectations increased. The changes suggest that the near-term relative rate outlook moved modestly in NZD’s favor rather than against it, although the comparison involves different pricing instruments and reference rates. Both central banks are nevertheless expected to tighten, leaving the absolute December rate outlook far from unambiguously supportive of Kiwi.

Nevertheless, the risk-aversion argument is stronger on the weekly horizon than in Tuesday’s intraday trading, when USD ranked weakest on the daily currency heat map. That distinction suggests the broader defensive environment has contributed to NZD/USD weakness without establishing that every move in the pair has been driven by Dollar demand.

AUD/NZD provides a useful cross-check. The cross has fallen approximately 2.8% from its October 28 peak near 1.2600, indicating that NZD has outperformed AUD since the RBNZ’s hold. That relative strength is consistent with a more supportive RBNZ rate outlook, particularly as markets assign only a small probability to another RBA hike in December.

The comparison reinforces the view that NZD/USD weakness is not primarily a New Zealand-specific monetary policy story. Kiwi has retained some relative support against Aussie even as both currencies have struggled in the broader risk-averse environment.

Risk Sentiment and US Data Remain the Immediate Tests

Attention now turns to US retail sales and Nvidia’s earnings announcement later Tuesday. Retail sales could influence the Dollar through expectations for US economic resilience and Fed policy, while Nvidia’s results may determine whether pressure on AI-related equities intensifies or begins to ease.

A sustained recovery in global equities accompanied by a NZD/USD rebound would support the interpretation that risk aversion has been the dominant driver. Continued Kiwi weakness despite stabilizing equities would instead put greater emphasis on Dollar demand, Treasury yields or other US-specific influences.

Further ahead, the RBNZ’s December 9 Monetary Policy Statement and the Fed’s decision later the same day will test whether relative rate expectations remain supportive of NZD.

ActionForex’s Technical View: NZD/USD,

NZD/USD’s decline from 0.5987 continued this week and hit the lowest level since 2020. It’s now entering an important zone, including 0.5484 (2025 low), 0.5467 (2020 low), and 61.8% projection of 0.5987 to 0.5564 from 0.5709 at 0.5447.

Some support could be seen around this zone to bring recovery. However, outlook will stay bearish as long as 0.5709 resistance holds, and risk will remain heavily on the downside.

Decisive break of this zone will confirm long term downtrend resumption. In this case, the next near term target will be 100% projection of 0.5987 to 0.5564 from 0.5709 at 0.5286.

In the monthly chart, outlook stays firmly bearish as NZD/USD continues to stay well below the falling 55 M EMA. Sustained break of 0.5467 would resume the whole downtrend from 0.8835 (2014 high). That would set up deeper medium to long term fall to 78.6% of 0.8835 to 0.5467 from 0.7463 at 0.4815, which is slightly below 0.4890 (2009 low).

Key Takeaways

  • NZD/USD fell to 0.54832, its lowest since 2020, approaching the 2020 low at 0.5467, despite RBNZ rate hike expectations rebuilding after October’s 4–3 hold.
  • OIS pricing implies about 2.96% for December 9 and about 3.69% by year-end 2027, so New Zealand policy is unlikely to be the main driver of the decline.
  • Global risk aversion is the more plausible explanation, with Nasdaq down 2.49% on Monday, VIX at 22.90 and the Aussie and Kiwi the weakest on the weekly heat map.
  • The support zone includes 0.5484, 0.5467 and 0.5447, and a decisive break would open the 0.5286 projection, while 0.5709 is the resistance for the bearish view.
  • US retail sales and Nvidia’s earnings (Tuesday) and the RBNZ and Fed decisions on December 9 are the next tests.

Stay ahead of NZD/USD’s test of the 2020 low and the risk signals that could decide it—join the ActionForex Telegram channel for regular market updates and analysis.

headline: Germany ZEW Sentiment Jumps to 35.6, but Recovery Remains Uneven
html_content:
Germany’s ZEW Economic Sentiment Index rebounded sharply from 28.1 to 35.6 in November, comfortably exceeding expectations of 28.3. The 7.5-point increase reversed October’s deterioration and signaled renewed optimism about the economic outlook. Assessment of current conditions also improved from -35.9 to -33.2, matching consensus, although the index remained firmly negative. The widening contrast between stronger expectations and still-weak current conditions suggests confidence in future improvement is running ahead of the recovery itself.

ZEW President Achim Wambach noted that “The German economy remains on its recovery track, albeit moving at a slow rate.” He pointed to increasing manufacturing orders and falling oil prices as potential supports for the upturn, but warned that government expenditure had been the principal driver of recovery so far, raising concerns about public debt sustainability. The improvement was also uneven across industries. Expectations strengthened in chemicals and pharmaceuticals, as well as electrical industries, while prospects deteriorated in metal manufacturing and the construction indicator moved deeper into negative territory. The sectoral divergence and dependence on fiscal support suggest the recovery remains fragile despite improving overall sentiment.

Eurozone expectations also strengthened substantially, with the ZEW Economic Sentiment Index rising from 18.5 to 26.5, exceeding consensus of 18.3. However, assessment of current conditions was virtually unchanged, edging from -14.8 to -14.7. The simultaneous improvement in German and Eurozone expectations points to a broader recovery in confidence, but the limited progress in current assessments underscores the gap between forward-looking optimism and present economic performance. November’s survey signals improving prospects rather than a decisive acceleration in economic activity, with the sustainability and breadth of the recovery still open to question.

Data Summary — ZEW Economic Sentiment, November 2026

Indicator Nov Exp. Oct
Germany Economic Sentiment 35.6 28.3 28.1
Germany Current Situation -33.2 -33.2 -35.9
Eurozone Economic Sentiment 26.5 18.3 18.5

Eurozone Current Situation

Indicator Nov Oct
Eurozone Current Situation -14.7 -14.8

Key Takeaways

  • Expectations rebound strongly: German and Eurozone economic sentiment both beat forecasts, pointing to renewed optimism despite persistently weak assessments of current conditions.
  • Recovery remains uneven: Improving manufacturing orders and falling oil prices offer support, but industry prospects diverge, particularly between chemicals, electrical industries and metal manufacturing.

text_content: Germany’s ZEW Economic Sentiment Index rebounded sharply from 28.1 to 35.6 in November, comfortably exceeding expectations of 28.3. The 7.5-point increase reversed October’s deterioration and signaled renewed optimism about the economic outlook. Assessment of current conditions also improved from -35.9 to -33.2, matching consensus, although the index remained firmly negative. The widening contrast between stronger expectations and still-weak current conditions suggests confidence in future improvement is running ahead of the recovery itself. ZEW President Achim Wambach noted that “The German economy remains on its recovery track, albeit moving at a slow rate.” He pointed to increasing manufacturing orders and falling oil prices as potential supports for the upturn, but warned that government expenditure had been the principal driver of recovery so far, raising concerns about public debt sustainability. The improvement was also uneven across industries. Expectations strengthened in chemicals and pharmaceuticals, as well as electrical industries, while prospects deteriorated in metal manufacturing and the construction indicator moved deeper into negative territory. The sectoral divergence and dependence on fiscal support suggest the recovery remains fragile despite improving overall sentiment. Eurozone expectations also strengthened substantially, with the ZEW Economic Sentiment Index rising from 18.5 to 26.5, exceeding consensus of 18.3. However, assessment of current conditions was virtually unchanged, edging from -14.8 to -14.7. The simultaneous improvement in German and Eurozone expectations points to a broader recovery in confidence, but the limited progress in current assessments underscores the gap between forward-looking optimism and present economic performance. November’s survey signals improving prospects rather than a decisive acceleration in economic activity, with the sustainability and breadth of the recovery still open to question. headline: Fed’s Musalem Calls for Several Rate Hikes by Spring as Inflation Risks Persist
html_content:
St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem warned that the Federal Reserve may need several additional interest rate hikes before spring 2027 to bring inflation sustainably back to its 2% target. Speaking on Tuesday, Musalem said, “The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve price stability in a timely manner.” He estimated that the current federal funds target range of 3.75–4.00% could be as much as 100bps below the level required to restore price stability. His assessment points to a potentially substantial tightening cycle ahead, with inflation still running above 3% and showing insufficient signs of returning toward target without further policy action.

Musalem argued that inflation persistence poses a greater risk than premature monetary tightening, particularly while economic growth remains above trend and current interest rates are not exerting significant restraint. “Inflation is too high,” he said, adding that “risks are skewed toward persistent above-target inflation.” His concern is that delaying further rate increases could allow elevated inflation to become more entrenched, ultimately requiring a more disruptive policy response. The remarks therefore frame additional tightening as necessary not only to restore price stability but also to prevent inflation risks from intensifying.

Musalem also emphasized the case for acting promptly while inflation expectations remain anchored. “Moving sooner, while inflation expectations are anchored, has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or economic growth,” he said. The Fed is scheduled to meet on December 8–9, with a 25bps increase currently expected. Although Musalem is not an FOMC voter this year, his call for several hikes by spring underscores the possibility that restoring price stability could require considerably more tightening than a single December move. His remarks highlight a policy debate increasingly focused on how quickly and how far interest rates must rise to contain persistent inflation.

Key Takeaways

  • Musalem calls for several hikes before spring 2027: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem argues that the current federal funds rate of 3.75–4.00% could be as much as 100bps below the level required to restore price stability.
  • Persistent inflation demands stronger restraint: With inflation running above 3% and economic growth remaining above trend, Musalem warns that risks are skewed toward prolonged above-target inflation, while current policy is not sufficiently restrictive.
  • Early action could limit economic damage: Musalem favors tightening while inflation expectations remain anchored, arguing that prompt action offers a better chance of restoring price stability without harming employment or growth. He is not an FOMC voter this year.
