headline: US Retail Sales Slow to 0.2%, but Ex-Auto Spending Shows Resilience
html_content:
US retail sales growth slowed from 0.8% to 0.2% mom in October, matching market expectations and signaling a moderation in consumer spending momentum. Total retail and food services sales reached USD 748.2B, up 6.8% from a year earlier. However, underlying spending proved firmer than the headline suggested, with sales excluding autos rising 0.6%, above consensus of 0.4%, after a 1.1% increase in September. Sales excluding both autos and gasoline stations also rose 0.5%, matching the previous month’s pace. The Census Bureau noted that the headline monthly increase was not statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90% confidence level, adding caution to the interpretation of October’s modest gain.

Motor vehicle sales were the principal drag, falling 1.6% after a 0.2% decline in September. Weakness also extended to several discretionary categories, with furniture and home furnishings sales dropping 2.3%, clothing and accessories declining 0.7%, and sporting goods, hobbies and books sales falling 0.7%. Food services and drinking places recorded a smaller 0.2% increase, down from 0.9% previously, suggesting more subdued growth in dining expenditure. However, the weakness was not uniform. Nonstore retailers posted another solid 1.2% gain following September’s 1.1% increase, while health and personal care stores and gasoline stations each recorded growth of 1.5%. The contrasting performances highlight uneven spending patterns across retail categories.

Despite the slowdown, October’s figures point to moderating rather than broadly contracting consumer demand. Total sales remained 6.8% above their year-earlier level, while sales over August–October increased 6.4% compared with the same period of 2025. More importantly, the continued 0.5% monthly increase excluding autos and gasoline suggests that underlying spending retained momentum despite weakness in major discretionary categories. Nevertheless, the figures measure nominal sales rather than inflation-adjusted consumption, limiting conclusions about changes in real purchasing activity. Overall, the report suggests that US consumers remain willing to spend, but growth is becoming more selective as strength in nonstore retailing contrasts with softer demand for vehicles, household furnishings and dining services.

Source: US Census Bureau, Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey, November 17, 2026. September comparisons follow the official Census release.

Key Takeaways

  • Headline growth slows, but underlying spending beats forecasts: Retail sales moderated from 0.8% to 0.2% in October, matching expectations, while ex-auto sales rose a stronger-than-expected 0.6%. Sales excluding autos and gasoline maintained 0.5% growth.
  • Weakness is concentrated in autos and discretionary categories: Motor vehicle sales contracted 1.6%, furniture sales fell 2.3%, and clothing and sporting goods declined. Meanwhile, nonstore retailers recorded another solid 1.2% increase, highlighting uneven demand.
  • Consumer demand moderates without broad contraction: Total retail sales remained 6.8% higher yoy, but the divergent category performance suggests increasingly selective spending. As the figures are nominal, they do not establish equivalent growth in real consumption.

headline: Dollar Firms After Retail Sales as Markets Await Nvidia and Trump–Xi–Putin Talks
html_content:
Dollar Firmed After Stronger Underlying US Retail Sales Ahead of Two Major Event Risks: Nvidia’s Earnings Tonight and Trump’s Thursday Meetings With Xi and Putin

Today’s themes:

  • Dollar strengthened after October US retail sales, which slowed from 0.8% to 0.2% mom as expected, while sales excluding autos rose 0.6% against consensus of 0.4%.
  • Nvidia reports tonight after Monday’s selloff, in which Nasdaq Composite fell 2.49% and S&P 500 lost 1.92%, with KOSPI down 2.59%, Nikkei down 1.34% and Hang Seng down 1.03% on Tuesday.
  • Trump meets Xi and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday, with Iran and Strait of Hormuz energy supplies in focus, while Brent traded around USD 93.57, within its USD 89–97 range.
  • The European Commission forecast Eurozone growth of 1.2% in both 2026 and 2027, with OIS pricing continuing to indicate approximately 24bps of ECB tightening on December 17.

Dollar strengthened following stronger-than-expected underlying US retail sales data on Tuesday, while global markets continued to digest Monday’s Wall Street selloff ahead of two major event risks: Nvidia’s earnings tonight and US President Donald Trump’s meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on Thursday. US Treasury yields remained relatively stable, while oil continued trading within its established range despite renewed volatility surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. Asian and European equities stayed under pressure, but the broader picture was one of consolidation rather than another decisive repricing across asset classes.

October US retail sales slowed from 0.8% to 0.2% mom, matching expectations, but sales excluding autos rose 0.6%, above consensus of 0.4%. Excluding both autos and gasoline, sales increased 0.5%, maintaining September’s pace. The underlying resilience provided a plausible catalyst for Dollar’s subsequent advance, with the latest currency heat map showing USD strengthening against most major counterparts. However, the broader spending picture remained mixed, as motor vehicle sales contracted 1.6% while nonstore retailers posted a 1.2% gain.

US Retail Sales: Softer vs Resilient

Softer signals Resilient signals
Headline sales slowed from 0.8% to 0.2% mom, matching expectations Sales excluding autos rose 0.6%, above consensus of 0.4%
Motor vehicle sales contracted 1.6% Nonstore retailers posted a 1.2% gain, and sales excluding autos and gasoline rose 0.5%, maintaining September’s pace

The Dollar Index had been little changed around 103.666 before the release, while US 10-year Treasury yield stood near 5.125%, down just 0.4bps. The yield had fluctuated within approximately 1bp for much of the session, indicating limited movement in rate expectations ahead of the upcoming events. In equities, Monday’s selloff saw Nasdaq Composite plunge 2.49%, S&P 500 lose 1.92%, and Dow Jones Industrial Average decline 1.41%. The weakness carried into Tuesday, with KOSPI falling 2.59%, Nikkei 1.34%, and Hang Seng 1.03%. European markets also declined, with FTSE 100, DAX and CAC 40 each losing around 1%.

Markets at a Glance

  • Dollar Index: little changed around 103.666 before the retail sales release
  • US 10-year Treasury yield: near 5.125%, down 0.4bps
  • Nasdaq Composite on Monday: down 2.49%
  • S&P 500 on Monday: down 1.92%
  • Dow Jones Industrial Average on Monday: down 1.41%
  • KOSPI on Tuesday: down 2.59%, closing at 4,968.49
  • Nikkei on Tuesday: down 1.34%, ending at 58,860.21
  • Hang Seng on Tuesday: down 1.03%
  • FTSE 100, DAX and CAC 40: each down around 1%

Follow Nvidia’s earnings, the Trump–Xi–Putin talks and Dollar’s post-retail-sales strength on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

Nvidia Earnings Set to Test Confidence in AI Trade

Nvidia’s earnings tonight represent the most immediate test of market confidence following the technology-led selloff. Shares of the AI chipmaker fell 4.12% on Monday, adding to concerns over the sustainability of technology valuations and the concentration of market exposure to AI-related investment. The results also arrive amid heightened scrutiny of the company’s governance and export-control arrangements, following Jensen Huang’s departure as CEO and the announcement of a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Asian semiconductor-sensitive markets reflected the pressure, although neither KOSPI nor Nikkei broke below its recent lows going into Nvidia’s results. KOSPI closed at 4,968.49, remaining above last week’s trough despite recording the sharpest decline among the major Asian indices. Nikkei ended at 58,860.21, staying within its recent trading range.

The distinction matters because the selling has been substantial without yet triggering fresh technical breakdowns in these benchmarks. Nvidia’s results could therefore become an important test of whether the AI-related decline stabilizes or extends further. KOSPI’s response in the following Asian session will be particularly relevant given its exposure to semiconductor shares. With the earnings announcement still pending, the immediate direction of the technology trade remains unresolved.

Trump–Xi–Putin Meetings Bring Geopolitical Risks Into Focus

Beyond Nvidia, attention is turning to Thursday’s meetings involving Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, particularly their potential implications for the conflict with Iran and energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz. The diplomatic discussions come against a backdrop of conflicting reports about shipping conditions in the Gulf, leaving uncertainty over whether tensions are moving toward resolution or further escalation.

Recent reports suggested that shipping flows through Hormuz had nearly recovered, but subsequent Iranian statements described continued closure of the US-backed southern route. Regional reports also cited tanker incidents, including a vessel struck by a projectile and Iranian claims that several tankers had encountered mines. Meanwhile, Trump said his administration was “very close to getting it done” on Iran, suggesting diplomatic efforts remained active despite the conflicting signals from the region.

Hormuz: Conflicting Signals

Easing signals Escalation signals
Recent reports suggested that shipping flows through Hormuz had nearly recovered Iranian statements described continued closure of the US-backed southern route
Trump said his administration was “very close to getting it done” on Iran Regional reports cited tanker incidents, including a vessel struck by a projectile and Iranian claims that several tankers had encountered mines

Oil prices have nevertheless remained within a relatively established range. Brent CFD was trading around USD 93.57, up 1.99%, while WTI stood near USD 86.62, up 1.85%. Brent has fluctuated broadly between USD 89 and USD 97 since retreating from above USD 100 earlier this month. The latest rise therefore represents movement within that range rather than a confirmed shift in the underlying trend, making it difficult to attribute the price change to any single geopolitical headline.

Oil at a Glance

  • Brent CFD: around USD 93.57, up 1.99%
  • WTI: near USD 86.62, up 1.85%
  • Brent range since retreating from above USD 100 earlier this month: broadly USD 89–97

Thursday’s discussions introduce a more consequential potential catalyst. Xi’s relationship with Iran gives the meetings particular relevance to the Gulf situation, although the extent of China’s influence on the negotiations remains uncertain. Progress toward de-escalation could ease concerns over energy supply disruptions, while unsuccessful discussions could prolong or intensify those risks. Until the outcome becomes clearer, oil’s established range provides a more useful indication of market conditions than individual intraday fluctuations.

Thursday’s Talks: Two Outcomes

Scenario Implication
Progress toward de-escalation Could ease concerns over energy supply disruptions
Unsuccessful discussions Could prolong or intensify those risks

European Commission Forecast Reinforces Existing ECB Outlook

In Europe, the European Commission’s autumn economic forecast offered little fresh direction for markets already focused on global equity weakness and geopolitical uncertainty. The Commission projected Eurozone GDP growth of 1.2% in both 2026 and 2027, followed by 1.3% in 2028. Inflation was forecast at 3.2%, 3.1% and 2.1%, respectively, pointing to persistent price pressures alongside subdued economic growth.

The outlook also highlighted differences between major economies. Germany’s 2026 growth forecast was raised from 0.6% to 1.3%, while France’s was lowered from 0.8% to 0.4%. However, these revisions did not coincide with a meaningful change in near-term ECB rate expectations. OIS-implied pricing continued to indicate approximately 24bps of tightening at the December 17 meeting, little changed from the previous reading of around 25bps. Around 44bps was priced by March and 69bps by October 2027.

European Commission Forecast and ECB Pricing at a Glance

  • Eurozone GDP growth: 1.2% in 2026, 1.2% in 2027 and 1.3% in 2028
  • Eurozone inflation: 3.2% in 2026, 3.1% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028
  • Germany’s 2026 growth forecast: raised from 0.6% to 1.3%
  • France’s 2026 growth forecast: lowered from 0.8% to 0.4%
  • ECB tightening priced for the December 17 meeting: approximately 24bps, against around 25bps previously
  • ECB tightening priced by March: around 44bps
  • ECB tightening priced by October 2027: 69bps

The limited repricing suggests the forecast largely reinforced an existing market outlook rather than introducing a new catalyst. European equities remained under pressure, but their declines were more consistent with the broader selloff following Wall Street’s losses than with a distinct reaction to the Commission’s projections.

The immediate market focus therefore remains on whether Nvidia can stabilize confidence in the AI trade, followed by whether Thursday’s diplomacy changes the risk outlook for Iran and oil. Dollar’s post-retail-sales strength adds a near-term currency development, while subdued Treasury yield movement and range-bound Brent suggest other markets have yet to establish a decisive direction ahead of those events.

Related Coverage

US Data and Fed Policy

  • US Retail Sales Slow to 0.2%, but Ex-Auto Spending Shows Resilience: US retail sales growth slowed from 0.8% to 0.2% in October, matching expectations, but the underlying figures were more resilient than the headline suggested. Sales excluding autos increased 0.6%, beating forecasts of 0.4%, while sales excluding both autos and gasoline maintained 0.5% growth. Motor vehicle sales contracted 1.6% and several discretionary categories weakened, but nonstore retailers posted another solid 1.2% gain. The report points to moderating and uneven consumer demand rather than a broad-based spending contraction.
  • Fed’s Musalem Calls for Several Rate Hikes by Spring as Inflation Risks Persist: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem warned that the Federal Reserve may need several interest rate hikes before spring 2027 to bring inflation back to its 2% target. With the federal funds rate currently at 3.75–4.00%, he estimates policy could be as much as 100bps below the level required to restore price stability. Musalem sees inflation remaining above 3% without further action and argues that current rates are not sufficiently restrictive. He favors acting sooner while inflation expectations remain anchored, potentially extending tightening well beyond the expected December hike.
  • Fed’s Hammack Sees Continued Tightening Need, Warsh Highlights AI Uncertainty: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack reiterated her preference for gradual interest rate hikes but warned that broadening inflation pressures and emerging labour market tightness could require greater monetary restraint. She argued that financial conditions are not yet sufficiently restrictive and attributed higher Treasury yields primarily to strong growth and Fed tightening expectations rather than AI-related corporate borrowing. Separately, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh highlighted AI’s potential to boost productivity and growth, alongside risks of employment disruption and disappointing investment returns, without offering near-term monetary policy guidance.

Europe and UK Data

  • Germany ZEW Sentiment Jumps to 35.6, but Recovery Remains Uneven: Germany’s ZEW Economic Sentiment Index jumped from 28.1 to 35.6 in November, comfortably beating expectations of 28.3. However, the Current Situation Index remained deeply negative at -33.2, highlighting the gap between improving optimism and weak present conditions. ZEW President Achim Wambach pointed to increasing manufacturing orders and falling oil prices as potential supports for recovery, while warning that government expenditure remains its principal driver, raising concerns about public debt sustainability. With industry expectations also diverging, the survey points to improving economic prospects rather than a convincing acceleration in activity.
  • UK Unemployment Falls to 4.6%, but Payroll Losses and Weaker Hiring Tell Different Story: UK unemployment unexpectedly fell from 4.7% to 4.6% in the three months to September, but ONS cautioned that changes in the Labour Force Survey sample partly explained the improvement. Other indicators painted a weaker picture, with October payroll employment declining by 34,000 and job vacancies falling to 690,000, their lowest non-pandemic level since 2014. Regular earnings growth also slowed from 3.7% to 3.5%, below expectations. The combination suggests that hiring demand and wage pressures are easing despite the better unemployment headline.

Australia and New Zealand Policy

  • RBA Minutes Reveal Hawkish Majority, but Three Dissenters Warn of Sharper Downturn: RBA minutes revealed a 6–3 decision to raise the cash rate to 4.85% in November, with the majority judging that existing monetary restraint was insufficient to address persistent inflation risks. Headline and underlying inflation are now expected to remain above 3% until late 2027, while stronger domestic capacity pressures, elevated oil prices and AI-related investment add to inflation concerns. However, three dissenting members favored waiting for the effects of previous tightening, warning that rising unemployment and the housing downturn could trigger a materially sharper economic slowdown.
  • RBA’s Bullock Flags Triple Inflation Threat from AI Spending, Oil and Expectations: RBA Governor Michele Bullock identified three major upside risks to Australia’s inflation outlook: accelerating AI and data centre investment, persistently elevated oil prices, and inflation expectations becoming entrenched above the central bank’s 2–3% target. She warned that AI-related spending is increasing demand for resources when the economy has limited spare capacity, while high energy costs could delay the expected easing in headline inflation. Early signs that businesses may regard 3–3.5% inflation as normal add to concerns about persistent price pressures, although Bullock also acknowledged downside risks from falling home prices and economic uncertainty.
  • RBNZ Survey Shows Near-Term Inflation Fears Rising, but Long-Term Expectations Ease: New Zealand’s one-year inflation expectations jumped from 2.60% to 2.92% in RBNZ’s November survey, while two-year expectations edged up to 2.36%. However, five- and ten-year expectations declined to 2.17% and 2.13%, suggesting longer-term inflation expectations remain relatively anchored. Respondents also raised their expected OCR to 3.05% at end-2026 and 3.40% over one year, indicating anticipation of further monetary tightening. GDP growth expectations improved, but the one-year house price inflation forecast dropped sharply to 0.51%, highlighting continued housing weakness.
  • RBNZ Sees Rising Global Financial Risks, but New Zealand Banks Remain Resilient: RBNZ warned in its November Financial Stability Report that global risks are increasing as geopolitical tensions, elevated government bond yields and stretched AI-related equity valuations leave markets vulnerable to further shocks. A correction could weaken New Zealand’s export demand, increase import costs and tighten offshore funding conditions. Nevertheless, banks maintain strong capital and liquidity buffers, while stress tests indicate that financial institutions can withstand severe disruptions. Domestic financial stress has eased but remains uneven, particularly among smaller businesses and sectors dependent on discretionary household spending.

NZD and AUD Crosses

  • NZD/USD Nears 2020 Low Despite Rising RBNZ Rate Hike Expectations: NZD/USD has fallen to its lowest level since 2020, approaching critical support at 0.5467, even as markets rebuild expectations for further RBNZ tightening. OIS-implied pricing has shifted higher over the past week, while the latest RBNZ survey shows rising near-term inflation expectations and a stronger anticipated policy-rate path. Yet global equity weakness and defensive currency demand appear to be outweighing that support. With NZD/USD approaching a major technical decision point, a decisive breakdown could expose 0.5286 and potentially revive the longer-term decline toward 0.4815.
  • AUD/JPY Targets 105.22 as Risk Aversion Favors Yen, RBA–BoJ Rate Gap Set to Narrow: AUD/JPY extended its decline toward 107.33 as global risk aversion supported Yen and weighed on Australian Dollar. The cross broke below the 107.63 Fibonacci projection, opening the way toward 105.22, with 103.90 a potential larger correction target. Meanwhile, OIS-implied expectations point to the RBA–BoJ policy-rate gap narrowing by approximately 72bps over the next 12 months, reducing Australia’s interest rate advantage. However, that convergence is already reflected in market pricing, leaving equity sentiment and defensive Yen demand as the more immediate drivers.

headline: Fed’s Williams Backs Further Rate Hikes but Sees No Need for Dramatic Action
html_content:
New York Fed President John Williams reaffirmed the need for further monetary tightening to contain persistent inflation, but pushed back against expectations of a more aggressive pace of rate increases. Speaking at the Axios BFD Annual Summit on Tuesday, Williams said, “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action,” adding that the Fed’s approach in recent months was “working well.” His remarks suggest support for another 25bps increase at the December 8–9 FOMC meeting rather than a larger 50bps move. Markets continued to price a December hike of 25bps with approximately 98% probability following his comments, which would lift the current federal funds target range from 3.75–4.00% to 4.00–4.25%.

Williams acknowledged that the economy remains resilient and the labor market is “solid,” but cautioned that “inflation, unfortunately, is not moving in the right direction.” October headline CPI rose 0.4% mom, above expectations of 0.3%, while core CPI increased 0.3%, also exceeding forecasts of 0.2%. September core PCE inflation accelerated from 3.0% to 3.1% yoy, reinforcing concerns about persistent underlying price pressures. Williams pointed to continued price increases in tariff-affected imported goods and the pass-through of higher energy costs, while identifying AI-related investment as a potentially more persistent inflationary influence. However, he stopped short of characterizing inflation pressures as broadening, distinguishing between specific sources of price increases and a more generalized deterioration.

The outlook for AI investment could also influence how far the Fed ultimately needs to tighten. Williams noted that AI spending is supporting economic growth, while stock market strength is helping sustain consumer demand. At the same time, investment in AI is contributing to price pressures in areas such as semiconductors. “If those continue, I think that that’s a factor that will argue that we may need to raise rates more,” he said, while emphasizing the considerable uncertainty surrounding the outlook. Williams maintained that the Fed still needs to bring inflation back to 2% “in a timely way and in a sustained manner,” but his rejection of dramatic action suggests a preference for gradual tightening rather than an immediate acceleration. The distinction is between the pace and the ultimate extent of tightening: a larger December hike appears unnecessary in his assessment, even as further increases beyond that meeting remain possible.

Key Takeaways

  • Williams favors further tightening, but rejects aggressive action: New York Fed President John Williams sees no need for a dramatic policy shift, pushing back against a 50bps December hike while supporting continued gradual rate increases.
  • Persistent inflation remains the central concern: Williams described the economy as resilient and employment as solid, but warned that inflation is not moving in the right direction. Tariffs, energy costs and AI-related investment are contributing to price pressures.
  • AI could influence how far rates ultimately rise: Williams identified AI as a potentially persistent inflation driver, with investment supporting economic growth and higher semiconductor prices, while stock market strength helps sustain consumer spending. The Fed’s tightening path will depend on how these forces develop.

headline: Japan Trade Deficit Narrows as Chip Exports Surge, but Oil Costs Stay High
html_content:
Japan’s trade deficit narrowed from a revised JPY 556.5B to JPY 476.5B in October on an unadjusted basis, as robust export growth helped offset a sharp increase in energy import costs. Exports accelerated from 16.5% to 20.5% yoy, exceeding expectations of 20.0%, while imports rose 21.6%, below forecasts of around 25.8%. Semiconductor-related products and automobiles were major contributors to export strength, with shipments of semiconductor manufacturing equipment surging 49.7% in value, semiconductors and related components also rising 49.7%, and motor vehicle exports increasing 19.9%. Nevertheless, the trade deficit remained wider than the JPY 301.9B shortfall recorded a year earlier, as higher import costs continued to absorb part of the gains from overseas demand.

Energy prices were a major source of pressure on the import bill, with the value of crude oil imports jumping 60.5% yoy despite a 0.7% decline in volume. The divergence highlights the impact of higher oil prices rather than stronger physical demand. Disruptions associated with the Middle East conflict have also prompted Japan to seek alternative supplies, with crude imports from the US surging 1,122.8% in value and 738.2% in volume. In contrast, shipments from the Middle East fell 16.5% by volume, even as their value rose 37.7%. The weaker Yen compounded the cost pressure, averaging 157.84 against Dollar in October, 5.6% weaker than a year earlier. NLI Research Institute economist Taro Saito identified elevated crude prices as the dominant factor behind the persistent deficit, warning that reliance on more expensive alternative supplies could keep the trade balance under pressure.

Export performance also varied considerably across destinations and industries. Shipments to the US rose 23.9% yoy, supported by a 37.2% jump in motor vehicle exports, helping Japan’s bilateral trade surplus widen to JPY 690.6B. Exports to China increased 13.3%, driven partly by a 42.6% rise in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, but motor vehicle shipments to China plunged 53.3% in value. Exports to the European Union also expanded 22.1%, reinforcing evidence of healthy overseas demand for Japanese goods. The contrasting trends underscore how strength in semiconductors and recovering US automobile shipments is supporting export revenues, while expensive energy imports continue to weaken Japan’s terms of trade. October’s narrower deficit therefore reflects strong export performance rather than a meaningful easing of import cost pressures, leaving the economy exposed to elevated oil prices and disruptions to energy supplies.

  • Energy import costs remain a major burden: Crude oil import values jumped 60.5% despite a 0.7% decline in volumes. Japan sharply increased purchases of US oil as Middle Eastern supplies declined, while Yen weakness added to import costs.
  • Export recovery differs across markets: US-bound motor vehicle exports rose 37.2%, while semiconductor manufacturing equipment shipments to China increased 42.6%. However, vehicle exports to China plunged 53.3%, highlighting significant differences across industries and destinations.

Full Japan trade balance release here.
text_content: Japan’s trade deficit narrowed from a revised JPY 556.5B to JPY 476.5B in October on an unadjusted basis, as robust export growth helped offset a sharp increase in energy import costs. Exports accelerated from 16.5% to 20.5% yoy, exceeding expectations of 20.0%, while imports rose 21.6%, below forecasts of around 25.8%. Semiconductor-related products and automobiles were major contributors to export strength, with shipments of semiconductor manufacturing equipment surging 49.7% in value, semiconductors and related components also rising 49.7%, and motor vehicle exports increasing 19.9%. Nevertheless, the trade deficit remained wider than the JPY 301.9B shortfall recorded a year earlier, as higher import costs continued to absorb part of the gains from overseas demand. Energy prices were a major source of pressure on the import bill, with the value of crude oil imports jumping 60.5% yoy despite a 0.7% decline in volume. The divergence highlights the impact of higher oil prices rather than stronger physical demand. Disruptions associated with the Middle East conflict have also prompted Japan to seek alternative supplies, with crude imports from the US surging 1,122.8% in value and 738.2% in volume. In contrast, shipments from the Middle East fell 16.5% by volume, even as their value rose 37.7%. The weaker Yen compounded the cost pressure, averaging 157.84 against Dollar in October, 5.6% weaker than a year earlier. NLI Research Institute economist Taro Saito identified elevated crude prices as the dominant factor behind the persistent deficit, warning that reliance on more expensive alternative supplies could keep the trade balance under pressure. Export performance also varied considerably across destinations and industries. Shipments to the US rose 23.9% yoy, supported by a 37.2% jump in motor vehicle exports, helping Japan’s bilateral trade surplus widen to JPY 690.6B. Exports to China increased 13.3%, driven partly by a 42.6% rise in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, but motor vehicle shipments to China plunged 53.3% in value. Exports to the European Union also expanded 22.1%, reinforcing evidence of healthy overseas demand for Japanese goods. The contrasting trends underscore how strength in semiconductors and recovering US automobile shipments is supporting export revenues, while expensive energy imports continue to weaken Japan’s terms of trade. October’s narrower deficit therefore reflects strong export performance rather than a meaningful easing of import cost pressures, leaving the economy exposed to elevated oil prices and disruptions to energy supplies. headline: Australia Wage Growth Jumps to 1.1%, Strongest Quarterly Rise Since 2023
html_content:
Australia’s Wage Price Index accelerated from a revised 0.7% to 1.1% qoq in the September quarter, exceeding market expectations of 0.9% and recording its strongest quarterly increase since December 2023. Annual wage growth reached 3.5%, compared with 3.4% a year earlier, although it remained below the 4.3% peak recorded in late 2023. The stronger quarterly result indicates renewed wage growth momentum, with the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) identifying increases under individual employment arrangements, enterprise agreements and award wage decisions as important contributors.

Both private and public-sector wages recorded substantial increases, rising 1.0% and 1.3% qoq, respectively. Annual private-sector wage growth reached 3.4%, while public-sector wages rose 3.9%, outpacing private-sector growth for the seventh consecutive quarter. In the private sector, the Fair Work Commission’s 4.75% increase to modern award rates from July 1, compared with 3.5% in the previous year, was a key driver. Public-sector growth was supported by enterprise agreement pay increases for state government frontline workers, including nurses, midwives and police officers. Although public wages rose faster, the private sector accounted for approximately 80% of the overall quarterly wage-growth contribution, reflecting its larger share of total wage expenditure.

The distribution of wage adjustments also pointed to firmer pay outcomes. Among jobs receiving wage increases, the proportion recording annualised rises above 4% increased from 24% to 34% over the past year, while the share receiving smaller increases declined. Health care and social assistance was the largest industry contributor, while New South Wales made the largest contribution among states, supported by pay rises for government employees. Nevertheless, the ABS noted that increases exceeding 6% remained below their 2023–24 peaks. The latest figures therefore show a meaningful acceleration in wage growth, but the prominent role of scheduled award adjustments and negotiated enterprise agreements suggests the quarterly increase should not be interpreted solely as evidence of renewed labour-market tightness.

  • Larger wage adjustments become more prevalent: Among jobs receiving wage increases, the share recording annualised rises above 4% increased from 24% to 34% over the past year. However, the prominent role of scheduled pay decisions means the acceleration does not necessarily indicate renewed labour-market tightness.

Speaking in parliament on Wednesday, Ueda said, “Given that financial conditions are still accommodative, it would be appropriate to continue raising the policy rate and adjust the degree of monetary […]
headline: BoJ’s Ueda Backs Further Rate Hikes, Warns Against Suppressing Bond Yields
html_content:
BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda reaffirmed the need for further interest rate increases, arguing that monetary conditions remain accommodative despite the central bank’s ongoing policy normalization. Speaking in parliament on Wednesday, Ueda said, “Given that financial conditions are still accommodative, it would be appropriate to continue raising the policy rate and adjust the degree of monetary easing in line with developments in the economy, prices and financial conditions.” The BoJ held its policy rate at 1.25% on October 30, while emphasizing a shift toward preventing inflation from overshooting its target. Ueda stressed the importance of anchoring underlying inflation around 2% over time, reinforcing the direction of further tightening without specifying when the next increase should occur.

Ueda also addressed the government’s proposed consumption tax cut on food, which he expects to support economic growth by improving households’ real purchasing power. However, the extent of the stimulus and its implications for underlying inflation remain uncertain, depending partly on how businesses adjust their prices and how consumers respond. A reduction in food taxes could ease the immediate burden on household budgets and provide room for spending elsewhere, but its broader impact would depend on the final design of the measure. Ueda said the BoJ would assess these effects once the details were finalized and incorporate the findings into future monetary policy decisions, without indicating that the proposal would necessarily change the pace of rate hikes.

On the bond market, Ueda distinguished between intervention to address serious disruptions to market functioning and purchases intended to suppress long-term government bond yields. He said emergency buying operations would require a comprehensive assessment of prevailing conditions, but warned that efforts to contain yields could backfire if investors interpreted them as central bank support for government financing. “In that case, long-term interest rates could become even more volatile,” he cautioned. The distinction underscores the importance of maintaining confidence in the BoJ’s monetary policy objectives while preserving the ability to respond to market dysfunction. Ueda’s remarks reinforce a continued tightening bias alongside a reluctance to use bond purchases simply to restrain borrowing costs, particularly where such intervention could undermine market confidence.

Key Takeaways

  • Further rate hikes remain appropriate: BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda reaffirmed that financial conditions are still accommodative and that policy rates should continue rising in line with economic, inflation and financial developments. He offered no timetable for the next increase.
  • Food tax cuts could support growth: Ueda expects the proposed consumption tax reduction on food to improve household purchasing power, but its effect on underlying inflation will depend on corporate pricing decisions, consumer sentiment and the final policy design.
  • Bond purchases could backfire if used to suppress yields: Ueda distinguished emergency intervention to address market dysfunction from attempts to restrain long-term borrowing costs, warning that perceived monetary financing of government expenditure could increase bond-market volatility.

headline: UK Inflation Rises to 3.6% as Fuel Prices Surge, Core CPI Holds Steady
html_content:
UK headline CPI inflation edged up from 3.5% to 3.6% yoy in October, matching market expectations, as higher fuel prices pushed inflation upward despite stable underlying price pressures. Monthly CPI rose 0.5%, compared with 0.4% in September, also in line with consensus. Core CPI inflation remained unchanged at 2.8% yoy, while services inflation held steady at 3.7%, suggesting the headline acceleration was not accompanied by a broader increase in underlying inflation. Meanwhile, CPIH inflation, which includes owner-occupiers’ housing costs, rose from 3.6% to 3.7% yoy.

Transport was the largest upward contributor to the increase in annual inflation, with its inflation rate accelerating from 6.6% to 7.5% yoy, driven particularly by motor fuels. Annual motor fuel inflation climbed from 29.8% to 33.2%, its highest level since July 2022. Petrol prices increased by 5.2 pence per litre in October, compared with just 0.7 pence a year earlier, while diesel prices rose by 7.0 pence against 1.2 pence in October 2025. Alcohol and tobacco inflation also accelerated from 2.5% to 4.5%, reflecting a 5.2% monthly increase in tobacco prices. The ONS noted that the timing of a tobacco duty increase, which took effect on October 1 this year rather than late November in 2025, may have contributed to the rise.

Offsetting some of these pressures, restaurants and hotels inflation eased from 3.8% to 3.4% yoy, providing the largest downward contribution to the change in headline CPI inflation. Food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation also slowed from 1.3% to 0.9%, its lowest rate since September 2021, helped partly by falling chocolate prices. Goods inflation accelerated from 3.2% to 3.5%, while services inflation remained unchanged at 3.7%. The latest figures therefore point to renewed pressure from energy and selected goods prices rather than a broad-based acceleration in inflation. Nevertheless, with headline CPI still well above the 2% target, stable core and services inflation offers some reassurance about the composition of the increase, but does not establish that underlying price pressures have decisively eased.

Key Takeaways

  • Headline inflation rises in line with expectations: UK CPI inflation increased from 3.5% to 3.6% yoy in October, matching forecasts, while monthly CPI rose 0.5%. Core CPI remained unchanged at 2.8% and services inflation held at 3.7%, indicating no corresponding acceleration in these underlying measures.
  • Fuel and tobacco drive the increase: Annual motor fuel inflation accelerated from 29.8% to 33.2%, its highest since July 2022. Alcohol and tobacco inflation also rose from 2.5% to 4.5%, partly reflecting the earlier timing of this year’s tobacco duty increase.
  • Food and hospitality provide offsetting relief: Restaurants and hotels inflation slowed from 3.8% to 3.4%, while food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation eased from 1.3% to 0.9%. The contrasting movements suggest October’s headline acceleration was concentrated in specific categories rather than broad-based.

Yields and the Dollar do not fully explain the scale of the selloff, pointing to positioning and broad commodity selling as possible amplifiers, with key support converging around 3,600–3,637.
headline: Gold Hits One-Year Low Ahead of FOMC Minutes as Fed Rate Path Takes Center Stage
html_content:
TL;DR: Gold has fallen to a one-year low ahead of the FOMC minutes, but the December hike is already settled and the bigger question is how far the Fed goes beyond it. Yields and the Dollar do not fully explain the scale of the selloff, pointing to positioning and broad commodity selling as possible amplifiers, with key support converging around 3,600–3,637.

Why Is Gold Falling to a One-Year Low Before the FOMC Minutes?

Gold extended its steep decline on Wednesday, falling to its lowest level in more than a year as investors prepared for the minutes of the Federal Reserve’s October 27–28 meeting. The metal was trading around 3,770 at 09:00 GMT, down more than 2% on the day and 6.5% over the past week. The broader backdrop remains unfavorable for bullion, with the Dollar near a 19-month high and markets pricing further Fed tightening. Yet the December rate hike itself is largely settled, with CME FedWatch assigning a 96.7% probability to a 25bps increase. The more consequential uncertainty is how far the Fed will need to raise rates beyond December. Meanwhile, gold’s latest decline is substantially larger than the Dollar’s advance, and Treasury yields are actually lower on the day, suggesting the selloff cannot be explained by interest rate expectations alone.

December Hike Nearly Certain, but Further Tightening Remains in Focus

The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75–4.00% in October, with the decision passing by a 10–2 vote. Governors Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented, both favoring a 25bps increase. The accompanying statement described economic activity as expanding at a strong pace while inflation remained elevated, reinforcing expectations that monetary policy would need to become more restrictive.

Since then, market pricing has shifted decisively toward a standard-sized December hike. According to CME FedWatch data at 07:53 GMT, the probability of a 25bps increase on December 9 stood at 96.7%, up from 95.5% on November 16 and 87.3% on November 11. Over the same period, the probability of a larger 50bps move fell from 12.7% to just 3.3%.

  • 25bps December 9 hike: 87.3% (Nov 11), 95.5% (Nov 16), 96.7% (today, 07:53 GMT)
  • 50bps December 9 hike: 12.7% to 3.3%

The shrinking probability of a jumbo hike does not indicate fading expectations for tightening. Instead, investors have become more confident about the immediate size of the next increase, while the debate has moved toward the number of additional hikes that may follow.

By the January 27 meeting, futures pricing implies approximately a 72% probability of another increase beyond December. Further along the curve, the expected policy rate is consistent with roughly 2.7 quarter-point hikes by April 2027 and 3.1 by November 2027, measured from the current range.

Recent Fed commentary has reinforced the prospect of additional tightening, although officials differ on how aggressively policy should respond. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has suggested that several rate increases may be required before spring 2027, with his assessment of the appropriate level of rates potentially exceeding what markets currently anticipate. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack has also argued that financial conditions remain insufficiently restrictive, while New York Fed President John Williams has supported further increases but pushed back against the need for dramatic action.

The minutes, due at 19:00 GMT, could provide greater insight into how broadly officials supported tightening at the October meeting, whether larger increases were seriously considered, and how policymakers assessed the eventual level of interest rates.

However, the document will be backward-looking. It predates October’s inflation report and the latest round of Fed speeches, limiting its ability to surprise investors unless it reveals a more hawkish or divided policy debate than currently understood.

Follow gold’s slide, the FOMC minutes and the Fed’s rate path on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

Gold’s Decline Outpaces the Move in Yields and Dollar

Gold’s recent weakness is broadly consistent with the repricing of Fed policy. Higher interest rates raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion, while a stronger Dollar adds pressure by making gold more expensive for holders of other currencies.

Over the past week, US two-year and ten-year Treasury yields have both risen by approximately 22–23bps, while the Dollar Index has gained 1.57%. These movements provide a reasonable macroeconomic explanation for part of gold’s 6.51% weekly decline.

But the relationship is much less convincing in Wednesday’s session.

At 09:00 GMT, gold was down approximately 2.06%, compared with a modest 0.22% increase in DXY. More importantly, the US two-year yield had slipped to around 4.791% and the ten-year yield to 5.093%, both down roughly 1.5bps on the day.

  • Past week: gold −6.51%; US two-year and ten-year yields +22–23bps; Dollar Index +1.57%
  • Wednesday, 09:00 GMT: gold −2.06%; DXY +0.22%; US two-year yield about 4.791% and ten-year yield about 5.093% (both about −1.5bps)

The divergence is also visible over a longer horizon. Gold has lost 9.46% over the past month, while the ten-year yield is only around 3bps higher over the same period. Although the benchmark yield has rebounded approximately 28bps from its early-November low, that recovery does not fully account for the scale of bullion’s retreat.

The Fed’s tightening trajectory remains an important source of pressure, but the latest decline appears too pronounced to attribute exclusively to rising yields and Dollar strength. Other forces may be amplifying the move.

Broad Commodity Selling Raises Questions About Positioning

The weakness extends well beyond gold. Copper was down 4.15% at the same market snapshot, while platinum and silver had fallen 3.45% and 3.39%, respectively. Crude oil was also under pressure, with WTI declining 3.36% and Brent losing 2.13%. Iron ore, up 0.18%, was a notable exception.

  • Copper: −4.15%; platinum: −3.45%; silver: −3.39%
  • WTI: −3.36%; Brent: −2.13%; iron ore: +0.18%

Silver’s sharper decline pushed the gold/silver ratio higher to 82.388, reinforcing the picture of broad selling across precious metals rather than an isolated adjustment in bullion.

Reuters cited analysts suggesting that investors were reducing positions and selling gold as a liquid asset. The simultaneous declines across metals and energy are consistent with such an interpretation, particularly given that gold has continued falling even as Treasury yields eased.

However, the evidence supports positioning or liquidity pressure as a possible contributor, not a confirmed explanation for the selloff.

Financial markets are not displaying a uniform flight from risk. South Korea’s KOSPI was up nearly 2%, Japan’s Nikkei was modestly higher, and European equities were showing relatively limited moves. Bitcoin and Ether were also down by less than 1%.

headline: Eurozone Inflation Confirmed at 4.0% as Energy Surges, Core CPI Revised Higher
html_content:
Eurozone annual HICP inflation accelerated from 3.8% to 4.0% in October, confirming the flash estimate, according to Eurostat’s final release. Consumer prices rose 0.5% mom, while core inflation, excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, edged up from 2.5% to 2.6% yoy, above the preliminary estimate of 2.5%. Headline inflation has nearly doubled from 2.1% a year earlier, although the latest increase was driven predominantly by energy. The upward revision to core inflation nevertheless indicates slightly firmer underlying price pressures than initially reported.

Energy remained the dominant driver of the headline acceleration, with annual price growth rising from a revised 19.0% to 21.0%, above the flash estimate of 20.8%. Its contribution to overall inflation increased from 1.72 to 1.89 percentage points, accounting for most of the rise in the headline rate. Other components also recorded more modest increases. Services inflation edged up from 3.2% to 3.3%, non-energy industrial goods inflation rose from 1.1% to 1.2%, and food, alcohol and tobacco inflation accelerated from 1.3% to 1.5%. Within the latter category, unprocessed food inflation increased from 4.0% to 4.6%, while processed food, alcohol and tobacco inflation remained unchanged at 0.4%.

Inflation developments varied considerably across member states. Italy recorded a sharp acceleration from 4.2% to 5.6%, while France’s rate increased from 3.4% to 3.7%. In contrast, Germany’s inflation eased from 3.3% to 2.9%, and Spain’s edged down from 5.0% to 4.9%. Across the EU, annual inflation rose in 16 member states, fell in nine and remained unchanged in two. The figures underline the uneven distribution of price pressures across Europe. While energy accounted for the bulk of October’s Eurozone inflation increase, the upward core revision and modest acceleration in services and goods prices suggest underlying inflation has not eased, even if its increase remains considerably smaller than the energy-driven headline rise.

Source: Eurostat, Euro Area Inflation, October 2026 Final, released November 18, 2026. September energy inflation and its contribution have been revised.

Key Takeaways

  • Headline inflation confirmed, core revised higher: Eurozone HICP inflation accelerated from 3.8% to 4.0% yoy in October, confirming the flash estimate. Core inflation rose from 2.5% to 2.6%, above the preliminary reading of 2.5%.
  • Energy accounts for most of the acceleration: Energy inflation climbed from a revised 19.0% to 21.0%, with its contribution rising from 1.72 to 1.89 percentage points. Services, industrial goods and food inflation also edged higher.
  • National inflation trends diverge: Italy’s inflation jumped from 4.2% to 5.6%, while Germany’s eased from 3.3% to 2.9%. The figures highlight uneven price pressures across the Eurozone despite the common energy-driven headline increase.

headline: Nvidia Beat Fails to Spark Rally as Shenzhen Summit Opens and Oil Stays Range-Bound
html_content:
Nvidia’s Results Initially Lifted Semiconductor Shares and US Equity Futures, but the Gains Moderated Through the Asian and European Sessions

What’s happening: Global markets showed only limited signs of recovery on Wednesday despite Nvidia’s stronger-than-expected earnings, with third-quarter revenue of USD 115.84B against USD 109.10B expected and fourth-quarter guidance of USD 130B against a USD 125.1B consensus. Nvidia’s after-hours gain narrowed from 4.82% to 2.91% by 12:38 GMT and Nasdaq futures from 1.37% to 0.79%, while Brent held around USD 93.19 within its USD 89.16–97.13 range despite fresh Gulf attacks, and DXY rose 0.29%.

Why it matters: Nvidia’s guidance already excludes China data-center compute revenue, so the shipment halt creates no additional shortfall, but lingering technology trade restrictions, a fragile US-China truce and lasting Hormuz risks are keeping investors cautious. The US session, the FOMC minutes later Wednesday and Thursday’s Trump-Xi-Putin summit will determine whether the tentative relief becomes a durable recovery.

Global markets showed only limited signs of recovery on Wednesday despite Nvidia’s stronger-than-expected earnings, as investors weighed lingering technology trade restrictions and geopolitical uncertainty ahead of Thursday’s Trump-Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen. Nvidia’s results initially lifted semiconductor shares and US equity futures, but the gains moderated through the Asian and European sessions. Meanwhile, fresh attacks in the Gulf failed to push oil decisively higher, even as the International Energy Agency warned that confidence in the Strait of Hormuz as a reliable energy corridor may have been permanently damaged.

The cautious response leaves markets facing several unresolved questions. Nvidia’s strong outlook has not dispelled concerns surrounding China’s access to advanced chips, while the Shenzhen gathering begins against a backdrop of fragile US-China trade arrangements. In energy markets, the threat of prolonged supply disruptions continues to compete with expectations of improving global supply availability. Dollar remained firm, with DXY up 0.29% and US Treasury yields modestly higher, while the FOMC minutes later Wednesday present another potential source of volatility.

Follow Nvidia’s fading relief rally, the Shenzhen summit and oil’s range on the ActionForex Telegram channel.

Nvidia’s Earnings Beat Brings Relief, but Equity Recovery Remains Limited

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of USD 115.84B, exceeding expectations of USD 109.10B by USD 6.74B. Its fourth-quarter revenue guidance of USD 130B also surpassed the USD 125.1B consensus, providing some reassurance that demand for AI infrastructure remains strong despite uncertainty over the company’s China business.

The outlook already excludes data-center compute revenue from China. Interim CEO Colette Kress confirmed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data-center products to Chinese customers, although she did not explain the reason for the halt. China accounted for USD 2.4B in sales of those products during the latest quarter, equivalent to roughly 2.1% of total revenue.

Nvidia Results at a Glance

  • Third-quarter revenue: USD 115.84B, against expectations of USD 109.10B, a beat of USD 6.74B
  • Fourth-quarter revenue guidance: USD 130B, against a USD 125.1B consensus
  • China Hopper data-center sales in the latest quarter: USD 2.4B, roughly 2.1% of total revenue
  • Outlook: already excludes data-center compute revenue from China

The exclusion means the shipment halt does not create an additional shortfall against Nvidia’s published guidance. Nevertheless, it highlights the restrictions surrounding one of the company’s important overseas markets, while unresolved governance questions following Jensen Huang’s departure remain another source of uncertainty.

Investors initially responded positively. Nvidia gained 4.82% in after-hours trading following Tuesday’s close, but its advance had narrowed to 2.91% by 12:38 GMT Wednesday. US equity futures followed a similar pattern, with Nasdaq futures advancing around 0.79% after having been up 1.37% Tuesday evening. S&P 500 futures were ahead just 0.32%, while Dow futures had slipped slightly into negative territory.

Asian markets also gave back part of their early gains. South Korea’s KOSPI opened 2.9% higher but closed up 1.99%, supported by a 5.1% rise in SK Hynix. Japan’s Nikkei finished just 0.28% higher after opening with a 1.1% advance. Hang Seng declined 0.91%, while Australia’s ASX 200 lost 0.69% for a fifth consecutive session.

Relief Rally: Early Gains vs Later Moves

Market Early gain and later move
Nvidia Up 4.82% after-hours following Tuesday’s close, narrowing to 2.91% by 12:38 GMT Wednesday
Nasdaq futures Up 1.37% Tuesday evening, narrowing to around 0.79%
KOSPI Opened 2.9% higher, closed up 1.99%
Nikkei Opened with a 1.1% advance, finished 0.28% higher

Europe remained subdued, with FTSE 100, DAX and CAC 40 all trading lower. The limited rebound followed two difficult sessions on Wall Street, during which S&P 500 and Nasdaq had lost approximately 2.9% and 3.2%, respectively, from Friday’s closing levels.

Nvidia has therefore provided a positive earnings catalyst without yet reversing the broader equity retreat. The US opening session will offer the next test of whether demand for semiconductor shares can support a more sustained recovery.

Shenzhen Summit Puts Trade and AI Technology Restrictions in Focus

The uncertainty surrounding Nvidia’s China business provides a direct link to the diplomatic agenda in Shenzhen, where Trump, Xi and Putin have gathered ahead of Thursday’s trilateral meeting.

Xi opened the APEC summit with a call for free and open trade, pledging further reductions in Chinese tariffs and improved access to domestic markets. Putin separately criticized Western sanctions, arguing that they had backfired on the countries imposing them.

Trump has arrived in China and was greeted by Xi at the airport before the three leaders participated in handshakes, photographs and a banquet. However, expectations for substantive progress remain limited, particularly on the trade and technology issues central to US-China relations.

The existing trade truce has been extended until January 2027, preserving reduced tariffs and some rare-earth trade flows. Yet several important commitments remain unresolved. A September agreement to reduce tariffs on USD 30B of goods on each side still lacks an implementation date, while China has linked additional purchases of US agricultural products to further tariff reductions.

New US restrictions on Chinese access to advanced AI technology have added another complication. Beijing has threatened retaliation, raising questions about whether the fragile trade arrangement can accommodate further controls on strategically important technology.

US-China Trade: Preserved vs Unresolved

Preserved or promised Unresolved or at risk
Trade truce extended until January 2027, preserving reduced tariffs and some rare-earth trade flows September agreement to reduce tariffs on USD 30B of goods on each side still lacks an implementation date
Xi pledged further reductions in Chinese tariffs and improved access to domestic markets China has linked additional purchases of US agricultural products to further tariff reductions
Trump greeted by Xi at the airport, with handshakes, photographs and a banquet New US restrictions on Chinese access to advanced AI technology, with Beijing threatening retaliation

For financial markets, the connection to Nvidia is particularly relevant. The company’s guidance suggests that its near-term revenue outlook does not depend on a resumption of Chinese data-center compute sales, but the restrictions remain important for the broader semiconductor industry and the future of technology trade.

Thursday’s meeting may therefore be judged less by the announcement of a comprehensive agreement than by practical signals on tariff implementation, technology restrictions and the preservation of the existing truce. With expectations already low, the absence of a breakthrough would not necessarily represent a new setback, but additional confrontation could complicate the limited improvement in market sentiment.

Oil Holds Range Despite Fresh Gulf Attacks and Lasting Hormuz Risks

Oil prices remained comparatively contained despite another series of security incidents in the Gulf.

Iran said it targeted US military facilities at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base, while a US military official described an earlier strike on Qeshm Island as retaliation for attacks on American personnel and assets. Bahrain reported intercepting further Iranian aerial attacks, and ADNOC Logistics & Services said one crew member was missing and 11 injured following an attack on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

Nevertheless, Brent was trading around USD 93.19 at 12:50 GMT, down 0.31%, after falling as low as USD 91.00 earlier in the session. WTI stood near USD 84.29, down 1.53%. Brent remained within its recent trading range of approximately USD 89.16–97.13, showing no decisive response to the latest escalation.

Oil at a Glance

  • Brent at 12:50 GMT: around USD 93.19, down 0.31%, after a session low of USD 91.00
  • WTI: near USD 84.29, down 1.53%
  • Brent recent trading range: approximately USD 89.16–97.13
  • Signal of a shift: a sustained move above USD 97.13 or below USD 89.16

The more important question may be how the conflict changes the energy market after the immediate disruptions subside.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol argued that confidence in Hormuz as a reliable shipping corridor has suffered lasting damage. He said he saw no credible return to the conditions prevailing before the conflict and warned that perceptions of risk surrounding the Strait had “changed for good”.

Birol pointed to alternative infrastructure, including Saudi Arabian and UAE pipelines that bypass Hormuz. These routes could become more important as producers and consumers seek to reduce dependence on a vulnerable shipping corridor.

The implications for oil prices are mixed. Persistent security risks could support a lasting geopolitical premium, but investment in alternative routes may gradually reduce exposure to disruptions. At the same time, the IEA’s reported assessment that Gulf crude exports had recovered to more than 80% of pre-war levels in October, alongside a projected fourth-quarter global supply surplus, provides a counterweight to upward price pressure.

Upward pressure Counterweights
Persistent security risks could support a lasting geopolitical premium Investment in alternative routes may gradually reduce exposure to disruptions

The market has yet to establish which influence will dominate. Brent’s continued movement within its established range suggests traders are balancing immediate geopolitical risks against the prospect of improving supply conditions.

Inflation Data

headline: Fed’s Waller Calls for 50bps December Hike Unless January Increase Is Signaled
html_content:
Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a potentially larger 50bps interest rate hike at the December 8–9 FOMC meeting, warning that inflation is moving in the wrong direction and becoming more widespread. Speaking to CNBC on Wednesday, Waller said, “I’m very, very concerned about inflation. It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.” He argued that restoring price stability may require a more forceful policy response, suggesting the Fed might need to “shock people” with aggressive tightening. His position contrasts with market expectations centered on a 25bps December increase, although Waller made clear that a larger move was not his only acceptable option.

Waller would also support a 25bps increase in December followed by another hike in January, provided the Fed clearly communicated that intention to markets. However, Chair Kevin Warsh has opposed such explicit forward guidance, arguing that it could constrain policymakers’ flexibility. Waller therefore sees a larger December increase as the alternative if the Fed is unwilling to signal another move. “If you’re not going to signal this very clearly to markets, you’re going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 [basis points] in December to put it in place and get it done,” he said. His argument centers on delivering sufficiently rapid tightening, either through one larger adjustment or two consecutive smaller increases.

Waller also argued that reversing the three 25bps rate cuts delivered in 2025 may not be enough to bring inflation sustainably back toward 2%. He questioned whether returning rates to their previous level would provide sufficient restraint, given that inflation had not been declining adequately before those cuts. The Fed may therefore need three hikes plus additional increases to restore price stability. His assessment highlights differences within the FOMC over the appropriate pace and extent of tightening. New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday that the situation did not require “dramatic action,” while St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has suggested several hikes may be necessary before spring 2027. The disagreement is less about the need for higher rates than about how quickly the Fed should deliver them and how much further tightening will ultimately be required.

Key Takeaways

  • Waller favors aggressive tightening: Fed Governor Christopher Waller warned that inflation is spreading and suggested a 50bps December hike may be necessary to deliver a sufficiently forceful response.
  • A conditional alternative to a larger hike: Waller would accept 25bps increases in both December and January if the Fed clearly signaled that path. Without such guidance, he prefers delivering 50bps immediately.
  • Further hikes may be needed beyond reversing past cuts: Waller argued that reversing the three quarter-point cuts from 2025 may not be sufficient to restore price stability, contrasting with officials who favor more gradual tightening.
